AFRST 146W-01: Black Women's Literary Renaissance

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Holman T
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-146, WMGST-146
💬 Comments: Open to First Years and Sophomores only.
📖 Description
The twenty-year period between 1970 and 1990 is often referred to as the “Black Women’s Literary Renaissance” due to the unprecedented amount of literary and cultural production from black women in the United States. This course explores its profound contributions to black life and literature. Students will examine the intersections and oppositions among political movements, such as the Lesbian Feminist Movement and the Black Power Movement, and identify how these connections shaped the aesthetic landscape of the time. Course materials will include essays, novels, poems, and visual art, featuring Alice Walker, Toni Cade Bambara, bell hooks, Lorna Simpson, and others.

AFRST 159-01: Elementary Jazz Dance

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Owens N
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats [Fr: 7, So: 6, Jr: 6, Sr: 6]
🔀 Cross-listed: DANCE-159
📖 Description
An introductory technique course exploring jazz dance as a form grounded in Black American cultural and performance traditions. Students develop foundational skills in rhythm, coordination, and jazz vocabulary while situating studio practice within the historical evolution of jazz dance. Attention is given to stylistic nuance, musicality, and expressive range within jazz movement. Open to all students; no previous dance experience required.

AFRST 201W-01: Diversity Reconsidered

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Carter D
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: AFRST-102, AFRST-112, AFRST-130, AFRST-190 or permission of the instructor
📖 Description
An examination of the emergence of Africana Studies as a transdisciplinary field of social and cultural critique and politics. Explores the work of foundational (e.g., W.E.B Dubois and Anna Julia Cooper) and contemporary figures. Topics include but are not limited to the history of Africana thought, race and global racial formation, resistance and politics, intersectionality, gender and sexuality, representation, white privilege, belonging, Blackness, and diaspora.

AFRST 224W-01: Gender, Space and Identity in the African Diaspora

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Merrill H
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: WMGST-224
💬 Comments: Open to Sr, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
This course examines how racialized and gendered identities are made in relation to space. How does gender intersect with race, class and other power relations embedded in the places we live? How do women and men come to occupy different places in the world – literally and figuratively – or occupy the same places in different ways? Case studies focus on identity making in relation to the body and the course more broadly focuses on the intersection of race, class, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity as matrices of social and structural power relations and hierarchies.

AFRST 232-01: Toni Morrison

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Holman T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-232
📖 Description
This course is an in-depth study of Toni Morrison’s fictional works and critical writing. Students will explore her creative and scholarly contributions to ideas of community and genealogy, as well as to representations of race, gender, and nation. Students will also explore her attention to language, form, and literary theory. In studying both Morrison’s formal and theoretical commitments, students will develop an awareness of how literature serves as a vehicle for animating and critiquing social, historical, and ethical concerns in our world. Assignments will include short critical essays, collaborative presentations and projects, and readings will include "The Source of Self-Regard," "The Bluest Eye," "Song of Solomon," and "Jazz."

AFRST 267-01: Jazz Connections

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ SCHA 108
👤 Instructor: Condon G
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: MUSIC-267/367
📋 Prerequisites: MUSIC 161/261, AFRST 161/261, MUSIC 257/357, AFRST 257/357, or consent instructor
💬 Comments: Not open to students who have taken MUSIC/AFRST 259/359. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor's permission.
📖 Description
An advanced jazz course that builds on the topics covered in Jazz Foundations (MUSIC 161), and examines the construction of the “jazz tradition” from a historiographical perspective. Considers how the development of jazz, and its construction in the context of educational institutions, both reflects and shapes concepts of race and gender in American culture. Includes an examination of the impact of jazz genres including hip hop, R&B, and gospel, and focuses on the international proliferation of jazz.

AFRST 335W-01: Urban Worlds

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Carter D
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Africana Studies or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores
📖 Description
Since the great northern migrations of the World War II era much of African American experience has been lived out in urban worlds, from New York to San Francisco. The city has held out a peculiar hope for a better life, celebrated in fiction, scholarly literature and popular culture, since the Black exodus from the South. We explore the American story of promise and inclusion and the visible and at times hidden workings of exclusion, two stories that unfold simultaneously in the experience of urban America.

AFRST 405-01: Seminar: Black Feminist Thought

Africana Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Emmert J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: WMGST-405
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Women's and Gender Studies or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Interdisciplinary examination of the tradition of black feminist thought as it spans African and African-American heritages. Exploration of how black women are not simply victims of oppression but visionary agents of change. Areas examined include history, literature,music,art,education, sociology and film. There is intersectional analysis of the social, structural, and institutional hierarchies within the identities of women of African descent (gender/transgender, race, white supremacy, sexual/affectional orientation, class, color, and ability).

AIIS 243-01: Indigenous Oral Traditions

American Indian and Indigenous Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Moss M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This course examines various elements of Indigenous oral traditions, including oral literatures like creation stories, narratives, cautionary tales, formal oratory, dance, and song, theorizing how some of these oral traditions can also be considered forms of writing. We will study different Indigenous methods of performance, analyzing elements such as tone and pitch, gestures, silence, back-channeling, turn-taking, taking of floor, and traditional openings and closings. We will also compare conversational norms, metaphors, puns, and humor used in diverse Indigenous cultures. Finally, we will examine the goals of decolonization in many Indigenous communities and explore the practices and discourses intended to decolonize and/or Indigenize daily life and promote Indigenous identities in the coming generations.

AIIS 262-01: Siberian Text

American Indian and Indigenous Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Abrahamyan A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-262, RSNST-262
📖 Description
This course is an exploration of five centuries of writing in and about Siberia. While we will root ourselves in the socio-historical context, our main goal is to engage meaningfully with the very process of the formation of the Siberian Text. By this, scholars of the region mean the body of works that emerged out of the geographical, political, anthropological, and cultural categorizations of Siberia. The plurality of voices and the diversity of spatial experiences engaged in the process of creating the Siberian Text include travelers, criminals, political prisoners, religious dissenters, shamans, hunters, ethnographers, missionaries, vagabonds, and peasants. Probing the fraught legacy of the current spatial discourse on Siberia, the course will examine a variety of media and genres, including official documents, travelogues, oral tradition(s), works of fiction, autobiographies, pictorial art, and film. In addition to the transnational and transhistorical dimensions, we will engage with theories of space and place, imagined geographies, and ecocriticism.

AIIS 310-01: Where Tradition Meets Modernity: Emergent Indigeneity

American Indian and Indigenous Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Burke B
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: AMST-105
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovaiton Co-Lab
📖 Description
This class will explore Emergent Indigeneity: how Indigenous identity is a dynamic and continually evolving process of redefining and making that rejects fixed notions of “purity” or “authenticity.” We will look at the ways modern American Indian and First Nations artists draw upon traditional practices, materials, and cosmologies within their tribally-specific knowledge systems, but use modern technologies, methods, and materials to communicate what it means to be Indigenous in the late 20th and early 21st century. For example, we might look at how Native writers redefine a literary genre drawing on specific Indigenous knowledge systems, how some Indigenous pop-music artists sample traditional songs, or how TV writers represent cultural practices in a modern context. Will include literature, film, TV, music, social media, and material culture, as well as beadwork, performance art, and modern art.

AMST 105-01: Introduction to Native American Studies

American Studies  •  1 Credit

Students learn about both historical and contemporary events and issues from Indigenous perspectives and develop new ways of thinking and talking about - and with - Native Americans.

AMST 117-01: Roots Music to Country Music: The Making of an American Sound

American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Hamessley L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]

📖 Description
Study of country music from its roots in cowboy songs, fiddle tunes, blues, bluegrass, and gospel hymns to current artists like The [Dixie] Chicks, Taylor Swift, and Brad Paisley. AMST 239-01: Native American Religious Freedom

American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Schermerhorn J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]

AMST 245-01: Music in American Film

American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ LIST 106  |  Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KRJH 125
👤 Instructor: Hamessley L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: MUSIC-245/345
📋 Prerequisites: Two courses in Music, Cinema and Media Studies, or Literature
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Years Three hours per week for film viewings in addition to class time. Music 345 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor’s permission.
📖 Description
Examination of music in American film from silent films to the present with emphasis on the golden age of Hollywood. Topics include the development of musical conventions in film, different approaches of film composers (Steiner, Tiomkin, Rózsa, Herrmann, Newman, Bernstein, Williams), the meanings that music brings to film narratives. Includes films such as Casablanca, The Adventures of Robin Hood, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, A Streetcar Named Desire, Amadeus, The Shawshank Redemption, Oh Brother, Where Art Thou? Special attention to Hitchcock films (Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window).

ANTHR 259-01: Digital Technology and Social Transformation

Anthropology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Ladousa P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One 100-level course in Anthropology or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
📖 Description
Examines some of the ways in which digital technologies have been imagined to be important to social change, transformation, or innovation. Proponents of the use of digital technologies toward social change have focused on their speed, connectivity, and capacity. The course will introduce some of these arguments, will review some critiques of these arguments, and will suggest – via ethnographic cases – that digital technologies, like all sociocultural forms, should be studied with careful attention to contextual concerns.

ANTHR 274-01: Medical Anthropology: Objects, Subjects, and Narratives

Anthropology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Kolarevic M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ANTHR-113
💬 Comments: Engaging with questions of power, knowledge, embodiment, and inequality, students will examine topics including medicalization, mental health, pharmaceuticalization, biological citizenship, structural violence, and the politics of life and death. Throughout the course, we ask how medicine both reflects and transforms the societies in which it operates.
📖 Description
Medicine does more than diagnose and treat illness. It produces knowledge about bodies, shapes understandings of health and disease, and influences how individuals experience themselves and others. This course examines medicine as a social, cultural, and political practice through three interconnected themes: objects, subjects, and narratives. Drawing on ethnographic research and critical social theory, we explore how medical knowledge is produced, how bodies become objects of scientific inquiry and intervention, and how medical categories and institutions shape identities, experiences, and social relations. We consider the material worlds of medicine, from pharmaceuticals and medical technologies to the human body itself; the formation of medical subjects through diagnosis, treatment, and care; and the narratives through which illness, suffering, and healing acquire meaning.

ANTHR 288-01: The Corporation

Anthropology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Ren C
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 4, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 4]
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-288
📖 Description
The Corporation examines how corporations have evolved as economic, political, and cultural institutions, shaping and reflecting the societies in which they operate. Drawing on historical analysis and ethnographic perspectives, the course traces their development from early chartered companies to the 2008 financial crisis, exploring key transformations in corporate structure, legal personhood, and financialization. We will consider how corporations have been shaped by historical forces such as colonialism, industrialization, and neoliberalism, while also analyzing their cultural logics, organizational practices, and symbolic power. Readings will examine how corporations have reshaped labor, culture, and economic inequality, as well as the ways they have been challenged and reformed. By examining corporate influence across time and space, students will gain a deeper understanding of its role in the modern world.

ANTHR 348-01: Anthropology of Audiovisual Entertainment

Anthropology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Chen S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ANTHR-113
📖 Description
This course explores how narratives and identities are constructed, mediated, and consumed through a combination of sound and image in audiovisual entertainment such as anime, cartoons, and video games. Drawing on anthropology, media studies, performance studies, and sociolinguistics, we will explore audiovisual entertainment not merely as a leisure consumption but as the means through which creative workers and fan-viewers co-operatively construe and (re)imagine social relations.

ANTHR 350-01: Anthropology of Play: Toys and the Politics of Playfulness

Anthropology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Wang C, Chen S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ANTHR-113
📖 Description
This course examines play as a serious social, cultural, and political practice. Drawing on anthropological theories of ritual, performance, materiality, affect, and infrastructure, we explore how play organizes social life across contexts, from children’s games and sports to toys, anime, video games, trading cards, and digital platforms. Rather than treating play as trivial or escapist, the course approaches it as a domain through which identities are formed, communities are sustained, economies are structured, and power is negotiated.

ANTHR 412-01: Food Justice in the Mohawk Valley

Anthropology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Starr J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ANTHR-113 or by permission of instructor
📖 Description
Students will grapple with the inherent tension between the fact that there are people who live in the area that don’t have enough to eat and the way that all attempts to mitigate social problems are inevitably informed by certain kinds of cultural/economic/political conceptual frameworks that often remain unexamined and/or invisible. As we work our way through the course readings, the students will be asked to pair up with a local organization that is working to alleviate food-related problems in the area. As they work with the organizations, the students will be tasked with examining the successes of, and the difficulties faced by, the institutions, including the ways that people complicate any implementation of a solution.

ARABC 210-01: Minorities in the Middle East: History, Religion, and Relations with Political Powers

Arabic  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Amir S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: MEIWS-210, RELST-210
📖 Description
This course explores how minority communities in the Middle East—Druze, ʿAlawites, Kurds, Yezidis, Armenians, Maronites, Copts, Assyrians, and others—have been formed and transformed from the late Ottoman era to the present. Beginning with the shift from imperial pluralism to nation-state “minorities,” it examines how religion, identity, nationalism, and political power shape communal identity and minority–state relations. Case studies span Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, addressing genocide, displacement, nationalism, citizenship, security, and diaspora. Drawing on history, anthropology, religious studies, and political science, students examine how communities negotiate identity, power, and recognition in a plural Middle East. This course examines historical and contemporary experiences of minority communities in the Middle East. Some course materials address difficult subjects, including genocide, mass violence, persecution, forced displacement, sexual violence, religious and ethnic discrimination, and war. These topics are approached in their historical and scholarly contexts and are essential to understanding the experiences of the communities studied in the course.

👤 Instructor: Rivas-Tello D
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 12, So: 8, Jr: 4, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only Occasionally two sections of this course are offered.
📖 Description
An introduction to the fundamentals of archaeology, with emphasis on human biological and cultural records. Topics include a review of archaeological field methods such as sampling, survey and excavation, and analytic methods such as dating, typology and formation processes. Three hours of class with lab exercises embedded within that time.

ARCH 229-01: Archaeology of Death

Archaeology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Hubbard E
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ARCH-106 or consent of instructor
📖 Description
While death is a human universal, the ways societies deal with death, bodies, and burial vary greatly. This course explores mortuary practices through the archaeological record and what they can tell us about ritual, social, economic, and ideological institutions in the past.

ARCH 243-01: North American Archaeology

Archaeology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ SCCT 2012
👤 Instructor: Rivas-Tello D
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ARCH-106 or consent of instructor
📖 Description
The history of Native American cultural development prior to European contact.Topics include the timing and effects of human entry into North America, ice-age adaptations, plant and animal domestication, agriculture and beginnings of complex societies. This course will also consider the contemporary debates archaeologists grapple with when interpreting the region’s deeper history.

ARCH 248-01: Archaeology of Water

Archaeology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ SCCT 2012
👤 Instructor: Hubbard E
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ARCH-106
📖 Description
Water is many things at once: a basic biological necessity, a sacred substance, and a source of political power. Today, water crises reshape lives around the world, from droughts and vanishing aquifers in North America and West Asia to the rising coastlines threatening communities in the Gulf Coast and Southeast Asia. This course examines multiple themes on water through archaeological and anthropological case studies, approaches, and concepts. We'll look at how humans have exploited, managed, and made meaning out of water for the last several millennia, from the earliest farming and herding societies to current concerns on climate and AI infrastructure.

ARCH 254-01: Crafting Culture: How Artisans Shape Society

Archaeology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM @ SCCT 2012
👤 Instructor: Rivas-Tello D
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ARCH-106 or ANTHR-113
📖 Description
How can crafting shape societies? This course examines how crafting is not only the production of handmade goods but also a deeply social practice embedded within geological landscapes, belief systems, and political economies. Drawing on key concepts in archaeology, anthropology, Indigenous studies, art history, and museum studies, students will analyze archaeological and ethnographic case studies on crafting practices (e.g., pottery production, textile weaving, beadwork) across various cultural contexts.

ARCH 511-01: Senior Thesis Project in Archaeology

Archaeology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 12:00 PM – 12:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Goodale N
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📖 Description
Continuation of participation in ARCH-551 with revision and expansion of the senior thesis. Honors in the concentration is partly dependent on an A- or better in the course.

ART 104-01: Introduction to Drawing

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 101
👤 Instructor: Alan M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
This course will introduce drawing as both a tool for generating ideas, and as an art form in itself. Classes will feature experiments designed to spark and sustain creative impulses, as well as more traditional drawing exercises to train the eye and hand. This will be a multidisciplinary approach, focusing less on perfecting a craft than on building communication skills through visual language. Through discussion and critique, students will develop critical skills and learn how to convey their concepts with simple mark-making.

ART 106-01: Introduction to Ceramics

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Wed 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 116
👤 Instructor: Murtaugh R
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph, and Juniors Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Handbuilding techniques will be employed to explore the sculptural possibilities of clay. A developed visual and conceptual vocabulary will accompany the technical aspects of ceramics through studio practice and class critique.

ART 107-01: Art and the Environment

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 116
👤 Instructor: Murtaugh R
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 2, Sr: 4]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph, & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Three-dimensional explorations will focus and reflect upon our relationship with the natural and constructed world. Emphasis on process and the language of materials will direct form, meaning, and the context of objects and installations created. A developed visual and conceptual vocabulary will accompany studio practice and class critique.

ART 109-01: Introduction to Sculpture

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 116
👤 Instructor: Brener A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 4, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
This course will provide extensive opportunities to develop observational, conceptual and technical skills in sculpture. Basic woodworking, assemblage, casting, carving and installation methods will be covered, while examining the unique demands and benefits of working in three-dimensions. Through lectures, discussions and critiques, students will delve deeply into what it means to make sculpture in the 21st century.

ART 113-01: Introduction to Media: Integrated Media and Emerging Practices

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Fri 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 143  |  Fri 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 124
👤 Instructor: Huff A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 2]
🔀 Cross-listed: DARTS-113 MUSIC-113
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph, Jrs, and Srs
📖 Description
This course will serve as an introduction to digital technology in contemporary art making as it relates to interactivity, collaboration, and emerging practices. Emphasis will be placed on hands on experimentation and exploration across disciplines. We will cover installation art, web art, digital and time-based art, and immersive environments. Students will gain an overview of emerging digital practices, collaborative production strategies and correlations to social, aesthetic and theoretical issues. Other topics may include virtuality, performance, cyborgs, and network culture.

ART 116-01: Introduction to Photography

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 144  |  Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 133
👤 Instructor: Boardman D
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs., Soph, & Juniors Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Fundamentals of photography through the use of both analog and digital SLR cameras, black and white darkroom techniques, film scanning and digital printing. Emphasis on development of technical and aesthetic skills, and the potential of the medium as a tool for artistic expression. Cameras will be provided by the College.

ART 160-01: Figure Drawing

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 208
👤 Instructor: Kuharic K
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 7, So: 7, Jr: 2, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Application of basic drawing principles to the representation of the human figure, with emphasis on anatomy and proportion. Examination of related topics such as the figure in the environment and portraiture.

ART 203-01: Introduction to Painting

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 207
👤 Instructor: Kuharic K
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph., and Jrs. Only Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Introduction to the study of the methods and techniques of oil painting, with emphasis on still-life, figures and landscape.

ART 213-01: Introduction to Video

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 144
👤 Instructor: Downey K
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 4, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: DARTS-213
💬 Comments: Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Introduction to fundamentals of craft and study of experimental video. Emphasis on developing ideas and conveying meaning through video art, working outside commercial traditions.

ART 221-01: Introduction to Animation

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 144
👤 Instructor: Downey K
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 4, Jr: 3, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: DARTS-221
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only
📖 Description
An introduction to the history, tools and language of basic animation styles. This course will trace the history of experiments in animated imagery from 19th Century photography through 20th Century film into 21st Century digital works. The class will cover basic techniques in Photoshop, Adobe Premier, and illustration and animation software interfaces.

ART 233-01: Introduction to Printmaking

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 206
👤 Instructor: Alan M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Sophomores, & Juniors only Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Exploration of printmaking's interdisciplinary nature, blending drawing and painting via traditional methods including notan, rubbings, monoprint, monotype, suminagashi, linocut, and woodcut. Production of relief prints, carved blocks, print editions and an accordion book.

ART 302-01: Advanced Photography: Analog Techniques

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 133  |  Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 144
👤 Instructor: Knight R
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ART-116
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores Normally offered every 3rd year.
📖 Description
Advanced investigation and study of the creative tools of black-and-white photography through the use of analog film cameras. Emphasis on medium and large format cameras, studio techniques and darkroom printing. Continued exploration of personal vision with emphasis on social and cultural contexts for photography.

ART 305-01: Advanced Painting: Figuration

Art  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Wed 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 207
👤 Instructor: Kuharic K
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ART-104 or ART-160
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
This course develops basic paint handling, visual syntax, and conceptual abilities pertaining to the figure in space. Students will examine historical and contemporary methods. Students will gain an appreciation of the physicality, emotional touchstones, and communicative power of paint. Students will explore varied genres within representation. including contemporary portraiture, history painting, the nude, and self portraiture.

ART 308-01: Advanced Sculpture: Form/Surface/Content

Art  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 116
👤 Instructor: Brener A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ART-107 or ART-109
📖 Description
This course explores form, surface and content at an advanced level, questioning how sculpture can most effectively engage the viewer’s mind and body. Students will develop their own studio practices while experimenting with a broad range of techniques, including carving in wood and wax; mold-making and casting in plaster, resin, and silicone; and digital rendering and 3D printing.

ARTH 101-01: Introduction to Art History

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM @ MUSM 201
👤 Instructor: Tillery L, Bair N
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years
📖 Description
This course is an introduction to the production, reception, and circulation of art in the modern world, from roughly 1450 to the present. We will examine art in its social, economic, and political context, while focusing on themes of artistic mobility and collaboration, as well as exchanges across cultures and media. Students will gain a basic understanding of visual vocabulary and literacy, and develop visual analysis skills by working with objects in campus and local collections.

ARTH 103W-01: Art of Advertising

Art History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Bair N
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-103
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores only
📖 Description
Advertising images are everywhere, beckoning us to look and believe their message. But how do such images actually work, and where do their visual strategies come from? This writing-intensive seminar equips students with the foundational skills of visual and contextual analysis necessary for the study of art and visual media. We will study how artists, designers, photographers, and advertising professionals created influential campaigns in print, on television, and online. Students will learn to analyze how images and text work together, how ads capture our attention, how they borrow from different visual traditions, and how they shape our desires, often through troubling visual conventions.

ARTH 152W-01: Intersections in Global Art

Art History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Tillery L
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only
📖 Description
In this course we will look closely at 25 objects (roughly one per day) that embody significant intersections among different cultures and/or periods. We will be learning about how to look at works of art and how to effectively express our thoughts about them in spoken and written words. All class sessions will be held at the Wellin Museum of Art, Burke Special Collections, or the College Archives to guide our object-based study.

ARTH 201-01: Artifact, Testament, and Monument: Asian Art Histories

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Menon A
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-201
📖 Description
An introduction to the rich art histories of Asia from the prehistoric period to the present, with an emphasis on the arts of China, Japan, Korea, India, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and Indonesia. With the study of select objects, paintings, sculptures, monuments, and associated social, religious, and political milieus, students will be introduced to major styles and traditions in the history of art across Asia and will engage with critical themes in the interpretation of Asian art histories.

ARTH 212-01: Black Conceptualism

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Herrmann M
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
📖 Description
From the 1960s to the present, Black artists have played a leading role in developing the experimental techniques of conceptual art. Across the Americas, Europe, and Africa, Black artists moved beyond traditional mediums like painting and sculpture to create artworks in the form of typewritten texts, logical systems, philosophical treatises, historical archives, video installations, and street performances. These methods were tied to a wide range of themes: the critique of racist institutions, research into suppressed histories, explorations of postcolonial and diasporic identity, and the embodied experiences of gender and sexuality. Readings will be drawn from art history, artists’ writings, and interdisciplinary scholarship in Black Studies.

ARTH 233W-01: Fantastic Beasts and the Indian Ocean World

Art History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Menon A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📖 Description
Premodern illustrations of the Indian Ocean World archive the vivid imaginings of early artists and unregulated mapmakers. We will examine how the vastness of the Indian Ocean and the enigma of life on faraway shores manifested in maps and illustrations. In addition to representations of the toothy fish, dragons, and beaked monsters of the seas, we will study the portrayal of otherness in visual narratives of the Indian Ocean World. We will also discuss the role of religion in the creation of these images, and consider the significance of their perception, reception, and circulation.

ARTH 274-01: Building Jerusalem: The Making and Remaking of a Holy City

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Van Loan T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: JWST-274, MEIWS-274
📖 Description
Since its foundation, the city of Jerusalem has been claimed materially and spiritually by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. This course will, through its art and architecture, trace the complex history of Jerusalem from ca. 957 BCE to today’s divided city. The art and architecture of the city is contextualized in a way that speaks beyond the often-used and simplistic tripartite manner of constructing identity and history in the city.

ARTH 284-01: Northern Renaissance Art

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Tillery L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: GERMN-284, MDRST-284
📖 Description
This course explores the distinctive ways in which art was crafted and consumed in northern Europe during the age of Renaissance and Reformation. We will examine paintings and prints, propaganda and princely splendor, and carved altarpieces and ceremonial armor against the backdrop of both city and court, while considering issues of religious function, social use, and the economic history of the arts. The course also fosters a critical awareness of the methods of art history by drawing attention to scholarship on Northern art that has, in many ways, laid the foundations for modernity.

ARTH 296-01: Global Contemporary Art

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Herrmann M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
📖 Description
Global Contemporary Art surveys the expanding definitions, contexts, and forms of art in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, paying particular attention to the significance of artistic agency, artists’ writings, globalization, the art market, and political engagement and social transformation.

ARTH 301-01: Avant Garde: Cinema as Theory and Critique

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 7:00 PM – 10:00 PM
👤 Instructor: MacDonald S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-301, LIT-301
💬 Comments: Not open to first-year students.
📖 Description
A history of alternatives to commercial movies, focusing on surrealist and dadaist film, visual music, psychodrama, direct cinema, the film society movement, personal cinema, the New American Cinema, structuralism, Queer cinema, feminist cinema, minor cinema, recycled cinema and devotional cinema. While conventional entertainment films use the novel, the short story and the stage drama as their primary instigations, experimental and avant-garde films are analogous to music, poetry, painting, sculpture and collage.

ARTH 318-01: Epic Tales: Storytelling in South Asian Art

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: TBA
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-318
📖 Description
South Asia’s extensive corpus of epics, fables, popular tales, and romances have found spirited visual expression in the region’s history of art and architecture. This seminar will analyze artistic choice and the role that it plays in how words are visually translated into images. We will examine a range of case studies from a period spanning over two thousand years to understand how artists shaped space, unfurled time, and materialized heroes and villains in painting and sculpture.

ARTH 336-01: Anthropocene Aesthetics

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Herrmann M
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
💬 Comments: Not open to first year students.
📖 Description
This seminar in contemporary art history and theory explores ecological art in the era of anthropogenic climate change. The course’s guiding question will be: what forms might an aesthetic experience of nature take when it no longer privileges the human observer, but rather cultivates an equality and reciprocity among all forms of life? Possible answers will be drawn from recent work in art history, Black studies, Indigenous studies, continental philosophy, and science and technology studies. The course’s topics will include: post-Enlightenment aesthetics of nature, biopower, vitalism, post- and anti-humanisms, plant philosophies, bacteria and fungi studies, and deep time. These theoretical frameworks will be complemented with case studies on a global array of contemporary artists.

ARTH 345-01: Postcolonial Theory and Islamic Art

Art History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Van Loan T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: MEIWS-345
📖 Description
How does the study of art and architectural history interface with colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial structures of power? This is a pressing question for those who study the visual cultures of the Middle East, a region in which these power structures have had considerable impact historically as well as in the contemporary moment. This class will consider from theoretical and practical vantage points how colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial systems and institutions have governed or influenced the methods of study, scope, and modes of display of historical art from the Middle East. Topics will include colonial-era collection and museum practices, Orientalism and its critics, post-colonial nationalist art historical discourses, cultural heritage in and during the ‘wars on terror’, and visual discourses of contemporary Islamophobia. Students may pursue research projects with objects or items from the Wellin Museum and/or the Michael Lang ’67 Special Collections and Archives.

ASNST 143W-01: The Sacred in South Asia

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Amar A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: RELST-143
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Years, Sophomores, and Juniors
📖 Description
What constitutes the sacred in south Asia? Is it a person, place, river, hill, temple or nature/ecology? Where and how did the notion of sacrality emerge in South Asia? Is it linked exclusively to religious institutions or is it found in the daily lives of people? This course will examine these questions by exploring the multiple religious traditions of South Asia and examining their essential beliefs, doctrines, institutions, rituals and popular practices through a study of texts, material culture, films and ethnographic accounts.

ASNST 161W-01: Sages of the Tao in Chinese History

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Wilson T
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-161
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, and 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Examination of the two most significant sages in Chinese history and the disciples and schools that traced their origins to them. Close readings of texts attributed to Laozi and Confucius, the conflicting interpretations of their teachings throughout Chinese history, and the proliferation of schools that claimed to transmit their Tao. An eminent historian once said, “Every era has its own Confucius; it’s just that there are many different Confucius[es] in any one era.” This adage, as we shall see, applies to Laozi as well.

ASNST 201-01: Artifact, Testament, and Monument: Asian Art Histories

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Menon A
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-201
📖 Description
An introduction to the rich art histories of Asia from the prehistoric period to the present, with an emphasis on the arts of China, Japan, Korea, India, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and Indonesia. With the study of select objects, paintings, sculptures, monuments, and associated social, religious, and political milieus, students will be introduced to major styles and traditions in the history of art across Asia and will engage with critical themes in the interpretation of Asian art histories.

ASNST 208W-01: Asian Temples in a Digital World

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Wilson T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-208, RELST-208
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Asian Studies, History, or Religious Studies
📖 Description
Examination of three aspects of Asian religions: temple as built space, ritual object (e.g., image, talisman, offering, etc.), and ritual practice as intentional use of objects and space. Students work in groups to research an Asian temple of their choice and curate a web-based exhibition of the history of and ritual practices conducted in their temple. Instruction in digital tools of collecting, analyzing, and representing materials in a web-based exhibition. Writing assignments include short essays and a final research project of the student’s design to be presented with text and images in digital form.

ASNST 232-01: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Yaseen S
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-232, HIST-232, MEIWS-232
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

ASNST 271-01: Mother Nature—Climate Crisis—Jainism

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Costello C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: RELST-271
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr No prior coursework on Religion or Asia is required.
📖 Description
How have people in India understood and interacted with mother nature? How do they conceptualize the environment and ecosystems? How do they deal with climate change and ecological disasters? What role does religion play in shaping human attitude to the mother nature? Focusing on Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, the course examines how Indian communities have engaged and negotiated their relationships with the natural world to consider themes including the conception of environment as sacred space, ethical living, non-violence, animal-protection, and food-culture.

ASNST 289-01: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Advani A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-289, MDRST-289, MEIWS-289
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Fifty years ago, the scholar Marshall Hodgson coined the term "gunpowder empires" to describe the introduction of new military technology by early modern Islamic kingdoms across Eurasia, specifically in Turkey, Iran, and India. Using this cultural framework to study the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal Empires, this course will focus on issues of imperial power and expansion, social and religious authority, protest and dissent, language and literature, law and ethics, paintings and architecture, as well as gender and sexuality. We will explore the historiography of these Islamic polities along with reading primary sources including court chronicles, local histories, political treatises, religious texts, and poetry in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit, Hindavi and other languages.

ASNST 318-01: Epic Tales: Storytelling in South Asian Art

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: TBA
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-318
📖 Description
South Asia’s extensive corpus of epics, fables, popular tales, and romances have found spirited visual expression in the region’s history of art and architecture. This seminar will analyze artistic choice and the role that it plays in how words are visually translated into images. We will examine a range of case studies from a period spanning over two thousand years to understand how artists shaped space, unfurled time, and materialized heroes and villains in painting and sculpture. This class has no prerequisites.

ASNST 346W-01: Madness, Lovesickness, and Jinns

Asian Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Advani A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: MDRST-346, MEIWS-346
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. First Years require instructor permission.
📖 Description
“Madness” evokes images of rambling, potentially violent, individuals on the margins of society. How did historical attitudes to insanity evolve in early modern and modern Eurasia? Were madpeople always ostracized or were they simply objects of sympathy and pity? What did hospitals and other networks of care and healing look like for mentally ill patients? In poetry, the pain of separation of the lover from their beloved produced lovesickness. Finally, demonic possession of the brain by jinns (Islamic spirits) was thought to cause madness. How can we understand the literary, religious and supernatural world of these actors without dismissing it? This course will take a holistic view of insanity while engaging with the rise of asylums or other lunatic institutions.

BIO 100B-01: Explorations in Biology: Frankenstein Fish

Biology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Chang W
👥 Capacity: 30 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 10, Jr: 3, Sr: 2]
💬 Comments: Students must concurrently enroll in a Bio100L lab section. Not open to students who have taken any other Explorations in Biology course.
📖 Description
A thematic course exploring five fundamental features of all biological systems, including structure and function, information flow, energy and matter, interactions, and evolution. As humans continue to exploit the ocean’s resources by overfishing, aquaculture and mariculture have become more and more important to meet human demands for fish proteins. This course will examine overfishing, genetically modified/engineered foods, and animal cloning and engineering to introduce fundamental concepts of ecology, ecosystems and conservation biology, genetics and molecular biology, and ethical issues.

BIO 100P-01: Explorations in Biology: The Evolution of Sex

Biology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Kahrl A
👥 Capacity: 30 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 10, Jr: 3, Sr: 2]
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors, Juniors, Sophomores, & 1st Years. Not open to those who took BIO 100*. Must also sign up for a BIO-100L section. Students must concurrently enroll in a BIO 100L lab section. Not open to students who have taken any other Explorations in Biology course.
📖 Description
A thematic course exploring five fundamental features of all biological systems, including structure and function, information flow, energy and matter, interactions, and evolution. How did sexual reproduction evolve? Why don’t all animals make clonal copies of themselves? How does sex shape selection and the evolution of plants and animals? How does sex influence human life and society? These are some of the questions this course will explore as we dive into understanding the origins of sexual reproduction across the animal tree of life.

BIO 200-01: Microscopy Fundamentals and Applications

👤 Instructor: Martin K

📖 Description
This course is a broad introduction to many common types of microscopy (bright field, confocal microscopy, electron microscopy). In addition to learning the theoretical foundations, students will also get hands-on practice with microscopes throughout the semester. The course will also cover the basics of digital image acquisition, processing, and analysis. Three hours a week, split between class and lab.

BIO 203-01: Biomaterials

Biology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Martin K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Any BIO-100 or consent of the instructor
📖 Description
Plants and animals create materials to accomplish their complex goals for survival and reproduction. These biological materials, from wood to silk to shells to fur, have diverse and unique physical properties. This course will explore the physical/engineering properties of biological materials. We will learn the basics of structural mechanics while asking how and why organisms create these materials.

BIO 311W-01: Evolution

BIO  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Kahrl A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: BIO-100, one 200-level BIO course
📖 Description
This course will cover the fundamental principles of evolution starting with the processes that generate variation within and between populations and building up to the patterns that result in speciation and macroevolution. Students will spend the semester learning this material while engaging in research projects that involve data analysis, visual and oral communication, and extensive scientific writing.

BIO 325-01: Immunology

Biology  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM  |  Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Tonc E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 0, So: 4, Jr: 7, Sr: 9]
📋 Prerequisites: BIO-211
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores This course will have an accompanying three hours of laboratory work per week.
📖 Description
This course introduces the cellular and molecular mechanisms of vertebrate immunity in health and disease. Topics include the evolution and organization of the immune system, innate and adaptive immune responses, immune cell development and communication, and the dysregulation and therapeutic manipulation of immune responses. Lectures, case studies, and primary literature will be used to explore fundamental immunological concepts and their applications to human health. Laboratory experiments will examine immune cell function and introduce current immunological techniques through guided exercises and independent projects.

BIO 330-01: Systems Neuroscience

Biology  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM  |  Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 3087
👤 Instructor: Myers A
👥 Capacity: 10 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: PSYCH-330, NEURO-330
📋 Prerequisites: Take BIO-205 / NEURO-205 / PSYCH-205
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.
📖 Description
The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

BIO 427-01: Seminar in Disease and Behavior

Biology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Townsend A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: BIO-237 or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Students must have Junior or Senior standing. Not open to students who have taken BIO 430.
📖 Description
The relationship between animal behavior and disease is bidirectional: behavior can affect the likelihood of acquiring a disease, and disease can subsequently alter behavior. In this class, we examine the fundamentals of animal behavior (e.g., sexual selection, kin selection, social evolution, communication and signals, reproductive strategies) and apply them to current research on the ecology and evolution of disease. Discussion of foundational readings and the primary literature.

BIO 429-01: Seminar in Cancer Biology

Biology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Bochkov I
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: BIO-211, BIO-248, BIO-249, BIO-334, or permission of instructor
📖 Description
Why have we not cured cancer yet? There are many good ways to answer the question. By the end of this course, you will be able to articulate a dozen valid explanations and reframe these challenges as future research, healthcare, and policy goals. Through analysis and discussion of recent primary literature, we will explore the complex genetics and epigenetics of the group of diseases we call malignant neoplasms. Topics include mutations that drive tumor progression, phenotypes of malignant cells, interactions of cancer cells with their environment, techniques for studying cancer biology, and therapies used in modern oncology.

CHEM 265-01: Inorganic Chemistry and Materials

Chemistry  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM

📖 Description
Topics in inorganic chemistry, including periodicity and descriptive chemistry of the elements, electrochemistry, transition metal coordination chemistry, and the structure and properties of solid state materials. CHEM 270-01: Biological Chemistry

Chemistry  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Martinie R
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 0, So: 25, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: BICHM-270, BIO-270
📋 Prerequisites: 190
💬 Comments: Students must also register for a CHEM 270 lab. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
📖 Description
A survey of the chemical and physical nature of biological macromolecules, including nucleic acids, proteins, lipids and carbohydrates; biochemistry of enzyme catalysis; bioenergetics and regulatory mechanisms. This course satisfies the second semester of a one-year General Chemistry requirement for post-graduate Health Professions programs, however, this course might not also satisfy a Health Profession program’s requirement for a course in Biochemistry.

CHEM 322-01: Physical Chemistry II

Chemistry  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Kramer W
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: BICHM-322
📋 Prerequisites: CHEM-190, MATH-116, and PHYS-105, PHYS-195, or PHYS-205
💬 Comments: The department recommends that students take 321 prior to 322. Three hours of lecture.
📖 Description
A study of the fundamental concepts and principles of thermodynamics and kinetics. Topics include statistical and classical thermodynamics, prediction of the direction and extent of chemical reactions, equilibrium, chemical kinetics, catalysis, and reaction rate theory.

CHEM 325-01: Physical Methods for Chemical Analysis

Chemistry  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Mon 12:00 PM – 12:50 PM  |  Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Hutchinson C
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Must have taken or be concurrently enrolled in either CHEM-321 or CHEM-322.
📖 Description
An integrated lecture-laboratory course in which students learn to design, build, and use instrumentation to study the physicochemical properties of atoms and molecules. Topics include the theory and practice of optical spectroscopy, thermochemical measurements of gases and condensed phases, and the measurement of reaction kinetics. Evaluations stress mastery of laboratory technique and communication of results with an emphasis on oral communication. Speaking-Intensive. One hour of lecture, three hours of laboratory.

CHEM 345-01: Organometallic Chemistry and Catalysis

Chemistry  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Brewer K
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CHEM-255 or CHEM-265
💬 Comments: Restricted to CHEM majors. 0.5 credit course; runs 3/29/27-5/17/27
📖 Description
Readings in the primary chemical literature pairing historical and modern papers to examine organometallic bonding, catalysis, and the experimental evidence used to validate catalytic cycles. One-half credit seminar.

CHEM 347-01: The Road to Silent Spring and Beyond: The Intersections of Environmental Chemistry and Literature

Chemistry  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Hutchinson C
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ENVST-347
📋 Prerequisites: One 200-level Environmental Studies or Chemistry course
📖 Description
An exploration of how environmental chemistry shapes environmental literature. Course material will include primary chemical sources as well as essays, novels, short stories, film, and other environmental literature. This course will look at both natural environmental chemistry as well as the chemistry of anthropogenic changes and compounds, such as pesticides. Students will interrogate and discuss these connections then use them to discover their own intersections with chemistry and literature.

CHEM 348-01: Science, Technology, and Society

Chemistry  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Brewer K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: PHYS-348
📋 Prerequisites: Restricted to Chemistry or Physics concentrators or permission of the instructor.
💬 Comments: Restricted to CHEM and PHYS majors. 0.5 credit class; Runs from 1/20/27 to 3/12/27.
📖 Description
An examination of the assumptions, paradigms, and hierarchies embedded in science and technology. This course will examine evidence pointing to the structure of hierarchies built into and from science and how those structures may result in inequalities for various groups participating in and affected by science and technology. Topics will vary but might include: the objectivity/subjectivity of science; how biases and social structures intersect with equity, diversity, and inclusion in science; and gender and race disparities in STEM fields.

CHEM 361-01: Advanced Organic Spectroscopy

Chemistry  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Rosenstein I
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CHEM-255
💬 Comments: 0.5 credit class; Runs from 1/20/27 to 3/12/27. One-half credit.
📖 Description
A study of advanced topics in NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry with a focus on practical interpretation of spectra. Topics include NMR theory, chemical shift, spin-spin coupling, dynamic NMR, 2D NMR techniques (COSY, NOESY, HSQC/HMQC, HMBC), methods of ionization in mass spectrometry, and interpretation of mass spectral fragmentation patterns.

CHNSE 120-01: Second-Term Chinese

Chinese  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM  |  Tue/Thu 12:00 PM – 12:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Huang T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CHNSE-110
📖 Description
This course is the second semester in introductory level of Chinese. The course will cover the remaining five units (Unit 6-10) of the learning materials, Basic Mandarin Chinese (Speaking & Listening; Reading & Writing). The course will help students further develop skills in Mandarin Chinese to conduct basic communication across ethnic, cultural and ideological boundaries and to develop an understanding of Chinese interpersonal behavioral culture. At the end of the course, students will be expected to perform in speaking, listening, reading and writing Chinese at a level of proficiency appropriate for continuing on to the intermediate level of Chinese courses. They should also demonstrate a level of cultural understanding suitable for correct performance of assigned tasks in Chinese.

CHNSE 243-01: East Asian Women in Film

Chinese  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Wang Z
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-243
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years.
📖 Description
This course examines portrayals of East Asian women in mainland Chinese, Hong Kong, Taiwanese, Japanese, Korean, and Hollywood films, with an emphasis on the post-#MeToo era. Through close analysis of narrative films and documentaries, students learn to investigate how gendered experiences of oppression, resilience, and resistance are represented, challenged, and reimagined in diverse cultural contexts. Combining film studies and gender studies, the course highlights both shared and divergent regional patterns and encourages students to consider how cinema shapes public debates on social change, agency, and justice. All films include English subtitles. Course requirements include film viewings, presentations, active discussion, a creative project, and a final paper.

CHNSE 446-01: Understanding Taiwan through Film

Chinese  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Wang Z
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CHNST-200 or permission of instructor
📖 Description
This course is an advanced-level Chinese language and Chinese-speaking culture course. It explores the complex cinematic depictions of Taiwan’s history, politics, and culture across the greater Chinese-speaking world. At the same time, it provides advanced-level Chinese language training. Through this dual focus, students will gain a nuanced perspective on Taiwan’s role in shaping cinematic narratives while gaining the language proficiency needed to participate fluently in discussions on both familiar and abstract topics, present structured arguments, and articulate in-depth analyses and sophisticated ideas in Chinese.

CLASC 115-01: Ancient Greek History and Culture

Classical Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: TBA
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 0]

📖 Description
An introduction to the legacy of ancient Greece through the study of history, literature, philosophy, and art. This course will also consider the influence of neighboring cultures on Ancient Greece, including the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and the Persians, to name a few.

CLASC 207-01: The Social Lives of the Ancient Dead

Classical Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Persad S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: RELST-207
💬 Comments: (Application, Interpretation)
📖 Description
What happened to people after they died in the ancient world? Often, their story was only beginning. This course looks at the ways the dead remained part of everyday life. We will read curse tablets that call on restless spirits, laws about stolen bodies, stories about cities fighting over heroic bones, and Christian accounts of remains that heal or protect the living. We will also study tombs and inscriptions to see how people used the dead to make claims about family, memory, status, and belonging. The course ends close to home. For the final project, students will turn to Hamilton’s own cemetery and investigate how one grave, monument, or burial story creates a social life for the dead on our campus. The larger question throughout the course is simple: what can the dead still do for the living?

CLASC 227W-01: Race and Ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome

Classical Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Feltovich A, Koenig A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: CLASC 227W is open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only. The 300-level is open to non-Justice Lab students with instructor's permission. This 200-level section is specifically designed to be part of a Justice Lab. Students who are interested in this course, but NOT planning to enroll in the Justice Lab, should consider the 300-level companion course, CLASC-327, offered by our department.
📖 Description
In this course, we will examine social constructions of race and ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome. What evidence survives, both textual and material, and what challenges do we face in interpreting it? How do conceptions of race differ by place and time through the Greco-Roman world? What is the difference between race and ethnicity? How have ancient ideas of race and racial hierarchies influenced later ones, and how have modern ideas influenced our interpretations of the past?

CLASC 327W-01: Race and Ethnicity in Ancient Greece and Rome

CNMS 103W-01: Art of Advertising

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Bair N
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-103
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores only
📖 Description
Advertising images are everywhere, beckoning us to look and believe their message. But how do such images actually work, and where do their visual strategies come from? This writing-intensive seminar equips students with the foundational skills of visual and contextual analysis necessary for the study of art and visual media. We will study how artists, designers, photographers, and advertising professionals created influential campaigns in print, on television, and online. Students will learn to analyze how images and text work together, how ads capture our attention, how they borrow from different visual traditions, and how they shape our desires, often through troubling visual conventions.

CNMS 145-01: World Films, World Faiths

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Rodriguez-Plate S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: RELST-145
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only Evening film screenings.
📖 Description
Introduces the practices and beliefs of several major world religions (including Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism) through the medium of film. Exploring Japanese anime, Indonesia documentaries, video films from Ghana, Bollywood mythologicals, Jesus-films from Latin America, Korean-Buddhist films, contemporary fictional glimpses into Jewish life, and more, shows how religious people live and struggle and find joy, by using the audio-visual medium of film.

CNMS 230-01: Bollywood Film

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Sundar P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-230
💬 Comments: This course may be offered as writing-intensive or not writing-intensive, per the deparment. Refer to the schedule for details.
📖 Description
The course charts a history of Bollywood, India’s mainstream Hindi-language film industry. Although dismissed for its use of melodrama and song-dance sequences, Bollywood has long engaged with other global cinemas and critiqued social, cultural, and political trends. Readings and films span romances about gender and nation like Mother India (1957) and Chaudhvin Ka Chand (1960); the 1970s "angry young man" oeuvre and its later avatars, crime and terrorist films; diasporic family dramas like Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003); and crossover hits like The Lunch Box (2013) that address the globalized present.

CNMS 232-01: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Yaseen S
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-232, HIST-232, MEIWS-232
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

CNMS 238W-01: The Films of the Coen Brothers: Genre and Pastiche at the end of the American Mythos

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM  |  Wed 7:00 PM – 10:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Schillinger S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-238
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Literature or Cinema and Media Studies, or permission of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment. Theory, Intermedia
📖 Description
This course will analyze the way the Coen Brothers’ films play with previously hegemonic myths about the American experience. How do their films negotiate expectations of genre? What happens to meaning when pastiche or appropriation become vital to the narrative and imaginary world of the films? We will watch up to a dozen films, including Fargo, No Country for Old Men, Miller’s Crossing, O Brother Where art Thou and The Big Lebowski, not quite in chronological order,. Readings from scholarly and theoretical material, as well as excerpts from many of their sources, from Homer to Hammett. We'll also consider some of the 20th century painting, architecture and style that informs their films. Mandatory out of class viewings.
