CNMS 289-02: Video Essays: Writing with Sound and Image

Cinema and Media Studies  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Sundar P
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-289
💬 Comments: 0.5 credit course; Meets 1/20/27-3/12/27 Open to Sophomores, Juniors, and Seniors.
📖 Description
Videographic criticism is a multimodal form of writing. In using sound and image to comment on audiovisual texts, the video essay blurs the line between object and method of study. This hands-on humanities lab introduces students to a wide range of videographic techniques and formats, and some of the theoretical and philosophical concerns driving recent developments in the field. Students learn to not only craft their own video essays, but display greater reflexivity about their aesthetic choices, interventions and compositional process. No prior editing or other digital experience required.

CNMS 301-01: Avant Garde: Cinema as Theory and Critique

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 7:00 PM – 10:00 PM
👤 Instructor: MacDonald S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-301, LIT-301
💬 Comments: Not open to first-year students.
📖 Description
A history of alternatives to commercial movies, focusing on surrealist and dadaist film, visual music, psychodrama, direct cinema, the film society movement, personal cinema, the New American Cinema, structuralism, Queer cinema, feminist cinema, minor cinema, recycled cinema and devotional cinema. While conventional entertainment films use the novel, the short story and the stage drama as their primary instigations, experimental and avant-garde films are analogous to music, poetry, painting, sculpture and collage.

CNMS 349-01: Queer and Trans Cultural Production

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Marvin A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: WMGST-349
📋 Prerequisites: A course in Women's and Gender Studies or Cinema Media Studies or consent of instructor
📖 Description
This course explores queer and trans cultural production, ranging from zines, film, novels, photography, television, short fiction, painting, fanfiction, installation, poetry, performance art, music, video games, and more. On one level, it offers an interdisciplinary investigation of queer and trans representation, and both the possibilities and limitations of positive images and mainstream LGBTQ visibility. On another level, we explore the ways that writers, filmmakers, and artists find meaning through LGBTQ cultural production and artistic practices. We will also consider the politics of publication and distribution. The course takes up an intersectional approach, thinking about how LGBTQ cultural production is shaped by gender, race, ethnicity, nationality, class, and ability.

CNMS 428-01: Post-War Cinematographic Memory

Cinema and Media Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Guyot-Bender M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: FRNCH-428
📋 Prerequisites: One French or Francophone Studies course at the 300-level or above
💬 Comments: Taught in French.
📖 Description
Based on three chapters of recent French history (the Occupation and the Holocaust; relationship with Algeria; May 1968 and social unrest), investigates how filmmakers mediate individual and national memories through moving images. The films will be considered in the context of recent historiographical material, theoretical discourse on cinema, and very specific cultural policies in France, as well as popular events around cinema. Includes about 10 movies. Some Friday afternoons will be reserved for film screenings.

COLEG 106-01: What is AI?

College Courses and Seminars  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Bejjanki V, Clark J, Ji C, Kucinskas J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
A hands-on first class in artificial intelligence, with no prerequisite knowledge of computer science or mathematics required. The course will cover the technical aspects, as well as the history, ethical implications, and societal impacts of artificial intelligence. Topics will span both the theory and practice underlying modern AI. Class is discussion heavy, consists of many hands-on projects and a synthesis project of the student's own design.

COLEG 239-01: Digital Human Rights Investigations Project

College Courses and Seminars  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Rivera S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
🔀 Cross-listed: GOVT-239
📋 Prerequisites: A 100-level course in Government or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Research based on Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) is a technique pioneered by non-profit organizations and academic institutions to improve the transparency and fact-checking of investigative journalism and strengthen legal cases in the area of international human rights. This course provides students with an overview of these techniques and considers associated ethical, privacy, and technological concerns. Students will use techniques learned in class to gather and analyze OSINT materials related to international human rights violations in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian War. There is a required field trip to Washington, D.C., which involves staying overnight.

COLEG 281-01: Common Ground: A Laboratory for Civil Discourse

College Courses and Seminars  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Seidule T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: GOVT-281, HIST-281
💬 Comments: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
📖 Description
Common Ground will be a speaking intensive, history and government class where students learn about the history of free speech in America and on campus through practicums. While engaging with the history, students will learn to disagree, agreeably through different exercises focusing on the U.S. Constitution in a "Reacting to the Past" role-playing game, a LLM for the Founding Fathers, and free speech on campus issues, especially the 2005 Ward Churchill incident that roiled the Hamilton campus.

CPSCI 101-01: Computer Science for All

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Wang W
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment. Three hours of lecture and two hours of laboratory.
📖 Description
The first course in computer science is an introduction to algorithmic problem-solving using the Python programming language. Topics include primitive data types, mathematical operations, structured programming with conditional and iterative idioms, functional abstraction, and objects. Students apply these skills in writing programs to solve problems in domains across the liberal arts. No previous programming experience necessary.

CPSCI 102-01: Design Principles

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Morrison-Smith S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-101
💬 Comments: Students must also register for a section of CPSCI 102 lab. Open to First Years and Sophomores only during registration. Remaining seats will be made available to Juniors and Seniors during Schedule Adjustment. Three hours of lecture and two hours of laboratory.
📖 Description
A second course in programming, concentrating on principled software design techniques. Topics include class design, effective functional decomposition, recursion, and structured data. Students will continue to develop programming proficiency by writing programs in the C++ programming language. Course discussion will emphasize, efficient implementations in terms of memory space and running time, computational complexity of algorithms, and an introduction to data structures.

CPSCI 130-01: Prealgorithms

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Chen S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📋 Prerequisites: Must have taken or be concurrently enrolled in CPSCI-102
💬 Comments: Three hours of lecture and two hours of laboratory.
📖 Description
Foundations of computational problem solving and mathematical techniques commonly used in computer science. Emphasis on analytical and logical skills, including an introduction to Boolean logic and proof techniques. Topics include set theory, permutations and combinations, mathematical induction, asymptotic analysis, recursion, regular expressions, searching and sorting, basic data structures, and graph theory. Topics are reinforced through extensive experiments in Python and Jupyter Notebooks, as well as a brief sojourn into functional programming. Prepares students for 200- and 300-level courses requiring mathematical underpinnings of computer science.

🕒 Schedule: Mon 2:00 PM–4:00 PM | 👤 Instructor: Ji C | 👥 Seats: 20
CPSCI 130L-2
🕒 Schedule: Tue 2:00 PM–4:00 PM | 👤 Instructor: Ji C | 👥 Seats: 20

CPSCI 220-01: Principles of Programming Languages

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 1:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Morrison-Smith S
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-102
💬 Comments: Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
📖 Description
Investigation into the nature, features, design and implementation of programming languages. Students will gain experience with a wide variety of programming languages through programming exercises. Topics will include, among others, object-oriented programming, functional programming, higher-order functions, type systems and polymorphism.

CPSCI 230-01: Algorithms and Data Structures

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Ji C
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-102; Students from the Class of 2029 and later must have taken CPSCI-102 and CPSCI-130
💬 Comments: Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
📖 Description
A study of fundamental algorithms and data structures from the canon, emphasizing correctness, and trade-offs between techniques, alongside deliberate coverage of topics from discrete mathematics. Topics include running time and space analysis, invariants as a means of proving correctness, and the divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming algorithm design paradigms. Specific problems include graph traversals, (optimal) sorting/searching, minimum spanning tree and shortest paths, longest common subsequences, balanced search trees, heaps, hashing, and union-find for disjoint sets.

CPSCI 250-01: Systems

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Doke K, Dong H
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-102
📖 Description
A study of computer systems and the distributed nature of modern computing. Through mastery of the material, students will become more effective programmers by gaining the ability to reason about different layers of software and hardware, enabling them to approach problem-solving through a wider lens. This course includes topics such as performance evaluation and optimization, memory organization and management, parallel and distributed computing, databases, filesystems, computer networks and protocols, and event-driven style programming. For their final projects, students will apply these concepts to build an interactive and distributed application. This course prepares students to take upper level systems electives, such as computer networks, operating systems, and computer architecture.

CPSCI 270-01: Artificial Intelligence

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Helmuth T
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-130
📖 Description
A survey of foundational and modern approaches to artificial intelligence. AI methods that tackle a variety of problems with no known efficient algorithms will be discussed, analyzed, and implemented. Students will learn to select an appropriate AI representation to solve a problem and empirically analyze the performance of their implementations. Students will learn to write technical reports explaining their systems and experiments. Topics include heuristic search, game AI, evolutionary computation, machine learning, and the ethics of artificial intelligence. Prepares students to take upper level AI electives.

CPSCI 330-01: Algorithms

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Chen S
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-230
💬 Comments: Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
📖 Description
A discussion of modern algorithms and advanced techniques, with analysis of time and space complexity in theory and practice. Topics will include, among others: geometric algorithms, graph algorithms, hashing, parallel algorithms, external memory algorithms, parameterized algorithms, and techniques for solving NP-hard problems in practice.

CPSCI 370-01: Natural Language Processing

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 1:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Wang W
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-220 and CPSCI-230
📖 Description
Introduction to the theory and implementation of Natural Language Processing (NLP). This course explores computational methods for processing, understanding, and generating human language. Students will learn to represent and process natural language, build and evaluate NLP models, and apply these models to real-world language tasks. Topics include text preprocessing and tokenization, language representations, text classification, neural language models, transformers, and large language models (LLMs).

CPSCI 390-01: Computer Networks

Computer Science  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Doke K
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: CPSCI-230; and must have taken or be concurrently enrolled in CPSCI-240
💬 Comments: Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
📖 Description
This course covers the fundamental concepts of data communication and computer networks. Topics include layered network architecture; reliable data transfer and transport protocols; routing and forwarding; data link layer communications and principles of shared media access. Advanced topics may include physical layer protocols, mobile networks, and software-defined radio networks. Students will apply their understanding of networking fundamentals while working on hands-on programming assignments.

DANCE 112-01: Elementary Contemporary Dance

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Avaunt C
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, and 1st Yrs No previous dance training required.
📖 Description
Studio-based course that introduces students to concepts and techniques of contemporary dance. Emphasizes movement articulation, kinesthetic awareness, and originality. Alongside developing movement fluency, students will learn to analyze and situate contemporary dance within historical and cultural contexts. The course explores how technique reflects cultural values and considers the frameworks through which we understand dancing bodies.

DANCE 114-01: Elementary Ballet

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Wilcox P
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. No previous dance experience required.
📖 Description
Beginner-level study of classical ballet with a focus on ballet's basic vocabulary in both barre and center floor exercises, studio-stage directions and designations for the classical positions of the body in space. Work on such stylistic aspects of ballet as musicality, dynamics and use of the head. Readings in kinesiology pertaining to muscular alignment analysis.

DANCE 159-01: Elementary Jazz Dance

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Owens N
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats [Fr: 7, So: 6, Jr: 6, Sr: 6]
🔀 Cross-listed: AFRST-159
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
An introductory technique course exploring jazz dance as a form grounded in Black American cultural and performance traditions. Students develop foundational skills in rhythm, coordination, and jazz vocabulary while situating studio practice within the historical evolution of jazz dance. Attention is given to stylistic nuance, musicality, and expressive range within jazz movement. Open to all students; no previous dance experience required.

DANCE 203-01: Movement and Meaning

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Avaunt C
👥 Capacity: 15 Seats [Fr: 4, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 3]
💬 Comments: No prior dance training required.
📖 Description
This course explores the moving body through multiple perspectives, examining how movement is shaped by personal experience, culture, and society. Drawing on philosophical and dance studies approaches, students consider movement as physical action while also attending to its expressive and cultural significance. Through experiential movement work, readings, written reflections, discussions, and presentations, students develop skills in observing, experiencing, and analyzing movement. Alongside this analytical work, the course emphasizes developing a stronger connection to one’s own body through physical exercises that support embodied awareness and healthy movement practices.

DANCE 213-01: Intermediate Contemporary Dance

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Owens N
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: DANCE-112, DANCE-113, or DANCE-114 or permission of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Sophomores, & 1st Yrs May be repeated for credit.
📖 Description
The study of contemporary dance incorporating technique and theory. Emphasis on alignment and efficiency of movement focusing on increasing strength and flexibility.

DANCE 215-01: Intermediate Ballet

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 12:15 PM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Larish M
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: DANCE-114 or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. May be repeated for credit.
📖 Description

DANCE 307-01: Making Dance II: Original Works

Dance and Movement Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM @ BLOD 101
👤 Instructor: Avaunt C
👥 Capacity: 25 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: DANCE-305 or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab
📖 Description
An intermediate choreographic course centered on the craft of composition: space, time, structure, texture, and dynamics. Through sustained studio practice, students will generate, organize, and refine movement material, exploring how compositional choices shape the experience of a dance. The course includes close study of professional choreography to inform students’ creative processes. It culminates in each student presenting a fully realized original dance work.

DARTS 113-01: Introduction to Media: Integrated Media and Emerging Practices

Digital Arts  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 143  |  Fri 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 124
👤 Instructor: Huff A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 2]
🔀 Cross-listed: ART-113 MUSIC-113
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph., & Jrs.
📖 Description
This course will serve as an introduction to digital technology in contemporary art making as it relates to interactivity, collaboration, and emerging practices. Emphasis will be placed on hands on experimentation and exploration across disciplines. We will cover installation art, web art, digital and time-based art, and immersive environments. Students will gain an overview of emerging digital practices, collaborative production strategies and correlations to social, aesthetic and theoretical issues. Other topics may include virtuality, performance, cyborgs, and network culture.

DARTS 231-01: Intermediate Media: New Frontiers in Storytelling

Digital Arts  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 143  |  Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 124
👤 Instructor: Huff A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: MUSIC-231, THETR-231
📋 Prerequisites: Any intro-level Digital Arts studio course, including cross-listed.
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab
📖 Description
This class will survey and create emergent and non -linear forms of storytelling using digital and hybrid tools. We will examine notions of narrative authority and hybridity in a digital age and think through different ways we might use technology to distill, break apart or reify modes of communication and visual metaphor. Discussion will push boundaries of traditional storytelling and consider connectivity, liveness and embodied presence. This course will draw on multiple forms of expression including but not limited to digital media, performance, sound, XR, web, and network environments.

ECON 266-01: Introduction to Econometrics

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM  |  Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Cross J
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-166 or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only. Not open to those who took ECON 400. Juniors must be ECON concentrator. Not open to seniors or students who have taken ECON 400.
📖 Description
An introduction to econometric methods that are frequently used in applied economic research. Emphasis on interpreting and critically evaluating empirical results and on establishing the statistical foundations of widely used econometric methods. Topics include the classical linear regression model, functional form, dummy explanatory variables, binary choice models, panel data models, instrumental variables and time series models. Three hours of class and 75 minutes of laboratory.

ECON 275-01: Microeconomic Theory

🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM

ECON 318W-01: The Economics of Technology and Innovation

Economics  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Georges C
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-166 or consent of instructor
📖 Description
An examination of the nature and implications of innovation and technological change. We will investigate the history and economic theory of innovation and technological progress, related policy debates, and future prospects. Particular attention to the implications of recent developments in information technology and robotics for labor markets and the distribution of economic wellbeing.

ECON 364-01: Financial Crises

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Couture C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-166
💬 Comments: For each crisis, we will explore the background leading up to the crisis, how the crisis unfolded, how policymakers responded, and the long lasting impact of the crisis.
📖 Description
An analysis of economic and financial crises including the Panic of 1907, the Great Depression, the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, and the Global Financial Crisis.

ECON 365-01: Economic Analysis of American History

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Tan J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-166
📖 Description
An examination and explanation of the development of the American economy, focusing on the period from 1840 through World War II. Topics include the economics of slavery and share cropping, the rise of big business, railroads and economic growth, the development of banks and the causes of the Great Depression.

ECON 379-01: Political Economy of Environmental and Energy Policy

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Cross J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-100 and ECON-166
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab
📖 Description
Markets, individual preferences, and political structures all play a key role in shaping environmental and energy policy. In this course, we will adopt a multi-level political economy approach that draws on behavioral economics to understand individual environmental preferences and works upward through electoral politics and institutional structures. Students will work with economic theory to understand predicted policy effects, and polling and congressional voting data to understand the factors that shape environmental policy.

ECON 380-01: Environmental Economics

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Tatro C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-166 or consent of instructor
📖 Description
An examination of issues in environmental policy from the perspective of economic theory. Topics include the measurement of benefits and costs of curtailing pollution and preserving ecosystems, the design of public policies to improve environmental quality, and the examination of past and current environmental programs in the United States and their success. Also considers sustainable growth and issues of environmental equity.

ECON 420-01: Economics of Education

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Ruebeck H
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-266 and ECON-275
📖 Description
A study of issues in the economics of education, using microeconomic theory and empirical methods to analyze K-12 education policy. Topics include: the determinants of school quality, how to find and retain effective teachers, the effects of school accountability programs on student achievement, the role of charter schools and school choice in the provision of high-quality public education, and the consequences of more widespread early childhood education. Students will learn to read and critique empirical research to understand its implications for policy, focusing on the experimental and quasi-experimental methods most commonly used by applied microeconomists.

ECON 421-01: Development Economics

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Conover E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-266 and ECON-275
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores
📖 Description
Students will learn about some of the challenges faced by people in developing countries, and about the tools used to assess the interventions designed to confront them. The course will be mostly empirical—students will critically read research papers and learned about the methods frequently used by applied microeconomists.

ECON 425-01: Financial Economics

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Couture C
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-266, ECON-275, and ECON-285, or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores
📖 Description
A study of individual level investment decisions and the equilibrium determination of asset prices. Mean-variance analysis motivated by the tradeoff between risk and return. An introduction to asset pricing models, including the CAPM and multi-factor models. An introduction to derivatives, including stock options, futures and swaps. Discussions of the Efficient Markets Hypothesis, arbitrage, and contributions from behavioral finance. Other topics may include: fixed income pricing, Arrow-Debreu securities and the completeness of markets, and the binomial asset pricing model.

ECON 505-01: Senior Project in Economic Development

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Conover E
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ECON-266 and ECON-275
💬 Comments: Open to Senior ECON Concentrators only. Instructor's signature required. Open to concentrators only. Co-requisite: ECON- 421
📖 Description
A senior project for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors. Students will work on projects related to the development economics.

ECON 516-01: Senior Project in Macro-Finance

Economics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM

ECON 520-01: Senior Project in the Economics of Education

Economics  •  1 Credit

EDUC 102-01: Issues in Education

Education Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Ladousa P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 20, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only
📖 Description
What is education? What is school? How do we critically understand education and schools? What are the possibilities and limitations of education for change and justice? Emphasis on, but not limited to, American education. Includes lecture, discussion, multi-media projects, and small-group interaction.

EDUC 203-01: Ethnography and Education

Education Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Starr J
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ANTHR-203
📋 Prerequisites: EDUC-102 or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph, & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
This course provides an understanding of the importance of ethnography to the consideration of issues introduced in EDUC-102. What is ethnography as a methodology for exploring education? Students will practice methods such as participant observation, interviews, and oral history through in-class exercises, as well as conduct an ethnographic project of their own.

EDUC 222-01: POV: You're Not the Main Character

Education Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Mansour K
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
What does it mean to listen to someone you disagree with? Why do some conversations bring people together while others deepen division? And can we learn to disagree without dehumanizing one another? In a time of polarization, cultural conflict, and competing ideas about belonging, this course explores dialogue as a practice for navigating difference and strengthening democratic life. Drawing on intergroup dialogue and critical theories of identity, power, and socialization, students examine how our experiences shape what we believe and how we understand others. Through storytelling, dialogue, reflection, and engagement with contested issues, students will learn to listen deeply, ask better questions, navigate discomfort and conflict, and connect interpersonal experiences to larger social systems. Ultimately, the course asks: If we understand one another differently, what becomes possible?

EDUC 370-01: Sociolinguistics of Globalization

Education Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Ladousa P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ANTHR-370
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Anthropology or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Explores the relationship between language variation and change, on the one hand, and the movement of sound and image in the wake of social and political economic processes variously identified as globalization, on the other hand. Of special concern are the ways in which processes of globalization are mediated by institutional and national forms.

EDUC 379-01: Lifespan Development

Education Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: TBA
👤 Instructor: TBA
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: PSYCH-379
📋 Prerequisites: Psych-201/Neuro-201
📖 Description
An introduction to the science of lifespan development, from conception and prenatal development to older age and death. Focuses on multiple domains of development, including cognitive, social, physical, and emotional, with emphasis on how development in all domains is shaped by both biological and social/cultural influences (e.g., gender norms, social class, stereotyping and prejudice).

ENVST 110-01: Introduction to Environmental Studies

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Strong A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 20, So: 20, Jr: 0, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only This course is a required component of the Environmental Studies concentration.
📖 Description
This course presents the core literature, theories, and concepts in environmental studies, with a focus on the emerging discipline of sustainability science. It will provide a comprehensive foundation for interdisciplinary study of contemporary environmental issues that will prepare students for more advanced work on the biophysical, social and human dimensions of environmental problems, including problems at the food-energy-water-climate nexus.

ENVST 151W-01: A Global History of Oil

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Ren C
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-151
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
📖 Description
How was our current dependence on petroleum created, and how can historical thinking help us imagine a better future? This course combines approaches from environmental and social history to examine the oil industry from the 19th century to today. Students explore social and environmental justice movements, the lives of oil industry workers, and our changing global economy, emphasizing peoples and places that are often marginalized. Contribute to contemporary debates on fossil fuels by analyzing museum exhibits in a final writing project.

ENVST 234-01: Environmental Justice

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Green A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 0, So: 6, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Africana Studies, Government, Environmental Studies, or Women’s and Gender Studies. Not open to first-year students.
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores
📖 Description
This interdisciplinary seminar examines environmental justice as a movement and concept. We interrogate and discuss the historical role of racism, heteropatriarchy, colonialism and globalization in (re)producing and justifying place-based environmental contamination and toxicity. Through close analysis of case studies in the US and the Global South, students analyze and present on how disenfranchised groups have made political demands, scaled up, forged solidarities, asserted climate justice, challenged state and corporate projects and conducted citizen science in rural and urban settings.

ENVST 234-02: Environmental Justice

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Green A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 0, So: 6, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Africana Studies, Government, Environmental Studies, or Women’s and Gender Studies. Not open to first-year students.
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores
📖 Description
This interdisciplinary seminar examines environmental justice as a movement and concept. We interrogate and discuss the historical role of racism, heteropatriarchy, colonialism and globalization in (re)producing and justifying place-based environmental contamination and toxicity. Through close analysis of case studies in the US and the Global South, students analyze and present on how disenfranchised groups have made political demands, scaled up, forged solidarities, asserted climate justice, challenged state and corporate projects and conducted citizen science in rural and urban settings.

ENVST 285-01: Introduction to Environmental Politics

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Cannavo P
👥 Capacity: 30 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: GOVT-285
💬 Comments: Students will explore these topics directly and through selected policy issues, including forest politics, sprawl and climate change. (American Politics)
📖 Description
An overview of environmental politics, domestic and global. Topics include the environmental movement and its history and values, anti-environmentalism, environmental policy analysis, the relation between environmental science and politics, the domestic and international environmental policy processes, the North-South debate, globalization, race and environmental justice, and the implications of environmental politics for liberal democracy.

ENVST 290-01: Nature and Technology

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Galusky W
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This course examines the sometimes contentious relationship between the natural world and human attempts to understand it (science) and control it (technology). We survey ethical, social, artistic and scientific distinctions between the natural world and the human-built world. Specific topics include everyday tools (e.g., hammers), food and agricultural practices (corn & chickens), modes of transportation (trains), and emerging biotechnologies (genes & humans). Readings will draw from works in philosophy of technology, environmental history, and science and technology studies.

ENVST 310-01: Seminar: Indigenous Ecologies

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Schermerhorn J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: AMST-310
📖 Description
This interdisciplinary seminar explores the traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) of indigenous peoples. Drawing upon scholarship from such diverse fields as acoustic ecology, ethno-ecology, ethnography, geography, environmental history, Native American and Indigenous Studies, and religious studies, we will examine indigenous knowledge about particular species and relationships between them.

ENVST 325-01: Environmental Data Science

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Kropp H
👥 Capacity: 15 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Must have taken ENVST 206 or an introductory statistics course in math or an applied discipline such as economics.
📖 Description
This course will focus on the application of statistical programming for big data associated with ongoing environmental issues. Students will gain experience in statistical programming throughout the entire data life cycle including data management and provenance, analysis, visualization, and communication. Students will learn the fundamentals of applying statistical modelling and machine learning for making predictions and inferences for environmental data. Students will also learn considerations of data science that are unique to environmental data including spatial, temporal, ethical, and justice concerns. Environmental topics will include climate change, pollution, natural disasters, and agricultural impacts.

ENVST 326-01: International Conservation Policy

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Green A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One 200 level or higher course in ENVST and/or PPOL
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores
📖 Description
This seminar course examines both the policy decisions and social justice issues that drive human actions and responses to international conservation challenges.

ENVST 327-01: Innovations in Environmental and Energy Policy

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Strong A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Co-Lab. Open to Co-Lab students only.
📖 Description
This experiential course examines barriers and bottlenecks to effective environmental and energy policy implementation and the proposed solutions and potential pathways to address them. Through case studies of climate, energy, water and conservation policy implementation, the course highlights the conditions under which innovation occurs and what the factors are that make it successful. Students meet frequently with local, state and federal policy practitioners, environmental and energy advocates and technologists. The course involves field trips to both Washington, D.C. and Boston to meet with environmental policy innovators.

ENVST 342-01: Sociology of Climate Change and Climate Action

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Strong A, Kucinskas J
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: SOC-342
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Environmental Studies or Sociology
📖 Description
In the face of the ongoing climate crisis, we are also witnessing deployment of climate solutions: electrification of transportation, renewable energy development, reforestation initiatives, and reductions in animal agriculture. How do communities react to these approaches to climate action? We unpack theoretical and on-the-ground perspectives on what climate change means among different groups of people and explore people’s social location influences how they understand and respond to it individually and collectively. We examine how colonialism, and macroeconomic structures shape perspectives on the experience of the climate crisis and responses to it. Students apply their theoretical understanding in structured community conversations about climate solutions with community stakeholders.

ENVST 347-01: The Road to Silent Spring and Beyond: The Intersections of Environmental Chemistry and Literature

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Hutchinson C
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: CHEM-347
📋 Prerequisites: One 200-level Environmental Studies or Chemistry course
📖 Description
An exploration of how environmental chemistry shapes environmental literature. Course material will include primary chemical sources as well as essays, novels, short stories, film, and other environmental literature. This course will look at both natural environmental chemistry as well as the chemistry of anthropogenic changes and compounds, such as pesticides. Students will interrogate and discuss these connections then use them to discover their own intersections with chemistry and literature.

ENVST 520-01: Senior Capstone Practicum

Environmental Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Kropp H
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Enrollment restricted to senior environmental studies concentrators.
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors Only. Restricted to ENVST Concentrators.
📖 Description
The course is summative and fulfills the Senior Program requirement in Environmental Studies. Building on previous coursework in the concentration, the capstone practicum focuses on developing and applying interdisciplinary research methods, skills and analytical tools to collaboratively understand and address environmental problems. Students conduct thematically linked, community-engaged research projects around a chosen salient environmental problem.

FRNCH 140-01: Communication in Francophone Cultural Contexts: Intermediate French II

French and Francophone Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Carbonnel P
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: FRNCH-130, placement exam, or consent of instructor
📖 Description
This intermediate-level French course is based on literary texts, news articles, films, and other related materials. Focus on speaking, listening, reading, and writing to express ideas and arguments with precision and nuance. Review of advanced grammar structures and expansion of vocabulary to develop strategies for description and narration and in expressing preferences and opinions, Analysis of texts and films develops critical thinking in French. Activities such as debates, interviews, discussions, and written assignments. Conducted entirely in French.

FRNCH 200W-01: Written and Oral Argumentation in French

French and Francophone Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Desjardins-Mooney Z
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: FRNCH-140 or placement exam; heritage speakers with instructor permission
💬 Comments: Heritage speakers with instructor permission. Regular class meetings plus a weekly discussion session with a teaching assistant.
📖 Description
An intensive course focusing on written and oral argumentation, proper nuanced expression, improvement of syntax and vocabulary-building strategies through the exploration of literary and cultural texts. Additional mandatory discussion session and activities.

FRNCH 212-01: Crime in French and Francophone Cultures and Fiction

French and Francophone Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Carbonnel P
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: FRNCH-200, appropriate score on placement exam, or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: May be retaken for credit. Taught in French.
📖 Description
Topics vary from semester to semester. From the 19th-century serial novel to Netflix success “Lupin,” dramas of life play out in French crime narrative that track transgressions, from affairs of the heart to atrocities committed by the government. This course examines works by figures ranging from convict turned policeman Vidocq, the real-life inspiration for Hugo’s Jean Valjean of Les Misérables, to Fred Vargas and Léa Slimani, two women who have revised the genre today. As we study the evolution of crime in literature since the early 19th century, we shall also consider the rise and manner of crime reporting in the French media and today’s cultural fascination with “true crime.”

FRNCH 250-01: Exploring Contemporary France: Current Events

French and Francophone Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Guyot-Bender M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: FRNCH-200, appropriate score on placement exam, or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Taught in French.
📖 Description
Exploration of selected trends and current events in the larger context of France’s historical, geopolitical and sociopolitical forces. The course alternates readings from a conventional textbook and various media covering current events. It makes use of text, images and sound. Topics include geopolitics; youth cultures; social, national and religious identities, labor laws, and the environment. There will be room to integrate debates likely to arise during the semester, especially around the presidential elections. Engaged participation in class discussion expected. Short written and oral assignments and a longer multi-media final research paper/presentation.

FRNCH 311-01: Contemporary French and Francophone Health Humanities

French and Francophone Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Desjardins-Mooney Z
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: FRNCH-211, or above; or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Taught in French.
📖 Description
This course serves as an introduction to contemporary French and Francophone health humanities. How have French and francophone authors portrayed health, illness, and medicine? How can medicine and literature inform one another, and in what ways can literary texts challenge the medical gaze and prevailing medical and psychiatric norms? Close readings of novels, poetry, letters, photographs, films, and medical writings. Attention paid to how dominant norms of citizenship, disability, gender, race, and sexuality shape medical science and discourse. Readings include works by Deligny, Duras, Ernaux, Guibert, de Kerangal, Malinconi, Manicom, and de Vigan, alongside theoretical texts by Fanon, Foucault, and Malabou.

FRNCH 428-01: Post-War Cinematographic Memory

French and Francophone Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Guyot-Bender M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-428
📋 Prerequisites: One French or Francophone Studies course at the 300-level or above
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors Only Taught in French.
📖 Description
Based on three chapters of recent French history (the Occupation and the Holocaust; relationship with Algeria; May 1968 and social unrest), investigates how filmmakers mediate individual and national memories through moving images. The films will be considered in the context of recent historiographical material, theoretical discourse on cinema, and very specific cultural policies in France, as well as popular events around cinema. Includes about 10 movies. Some Friday afternoons will be reserved for film screenings.

GEOSC 112-01: Principles of Geoscience: The Marine Environment

Geosciences  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM @ SCCT 1011  |  Thu 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM @ SCCT 1011
👤 Instructor: Kusnerik K
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 14, So: 10, Jr: 0, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only Three hours of class and two hours of laboratory, TBA. Not open to students who have taken any other course in Principles of Geoscience.
📖 Description
An introduction to the physical, chemical and biological nature of the marine environment. Topics include marine geology, seawater composition, atmosphere/climate, ocean circulation, waves, tides, coastal processes, life in the sea, ocean resources and marine pollution.

GEOSC 115-01: Principles of Geoscience: Evolution and the Environment

Geosciences  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM @ SCCT 1035  |  Mon 1:00 PM – 3:00 PM @ SCCT 1035
👤 Instructor: Beck C
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 14, So: 10, Jr: 0, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only Three hours of class and two hours of laboratory. Not open to students who have taken any other course in Principles of Geoscience.
📖 Description
This course looks at the intersection of life and earth history as a lens for understanding fundamental concepts in geology. Evolution will be studied on multiple scales from the origins of life in deep time, to hominin evolution in the Quaternary, to looking ahead to how we may have to culturally evolve in the face of anthropogenic climate change.

GEOSC 209-01: Hydrogeology

Geosciences  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM @ SCCT 1030  |  Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 1030
👤 Instructor: Jonathan S
👥 Capacity: 15 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One Principles of Geoscience course.
💬 Comments: The course consists of three hours of class and three hours of laboratory every week, with some outdoor field trips.
📖 Description
Hydrogeology is the study of surface water and groundwater, with a focus on groundwater. The course covers how water enters the subsurface, how groundwater interacts with surface water and flows in the subsurface through aquifers, and how it interacts with the surrounding soil and rock, affecting water chemistry. The course prepares students to address many environmental challenges that hydrogeologists study, including sustainable water supply, food and energy production, environmental protection and conservation, groundwater contamination, and climate change. The course prepares students to address such challenges by developing their ability to investigate groundwater systems, perform common laboratory and field methods, and solve complex problems in hydrogeology.

GEOSC 220-01: Earth Materials

Geosciences  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM @ SCCT 1033  |  Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 1033
👤 Instructor: Moser A
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Principles of Geoscience
💬 Comments: Three hours of class and three hours of lab with a field trip.
📖 Description
Minerals and rocks are the fundamental building blocks of planet Earth. This course will cover the physical and chemical properties of minerals and rocks, as well as the fundamental role that these “Earth Materials” play in the Earth system and their relevance to society.

GEOSC 223-01: The Critical Zone

Geosciences  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ SCCT 1030
👤 Instructor: Jonathan S
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 6, Jr: 6, Sr: 6]
📋 Prerequisites: One 100-level Geosciences course or permission of instructor
📖 Description
This course explores the science behind the critical zone, the dynamic zone at earth’s surface that extends from the base of weathered bedrock to the top of the vegetation canopy and encompasses the intersection of rock, soil, water, air, and life. Throughout this course, we will investigate the complex processes that drive the movement of materials through our environment and shape ecosystems and human societies. Examples of topics include soils and soil formation, nutrient cycling, and rock-climate interactions.

GEOSC 230-01: Structural Geology and Tectonics

Geosciences  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ SCCT 1016  |  Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 1016
👤 Instructor: Roberts N
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Principles of Geoscience.
📖 Description
An introduction to concepts of deformation of the lithosphere and the processes and products of rock deformation from microscopic to plate scales. Neotectonics as well as reconstruction of geologic history from the record of deformed rocks. Six hours of class/laboratory with field trip.

Geosciences  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Wed 2:30 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 1011
👤 Instructor: Kusnerik K
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors Only
📖 Description
A half-credit seminar to be taken in conjunction with GEOSC 511 (Senior Project). In this course students will continue to examine, discuss, and reflect upon structural and institutional hierarchies in the geosciences based on the social categories of race, class, gender, ethnicity, nationality, religion, sexuality, age, and/or disabilities. Students will also discuss ethical issues related to work and behavior as geoscience professionals. This seminar, taken along with its companion fall semester seminar (GEOSC 551) will satisfy the department’s SSIH requirement.

GERMN 284-01: Northern Renaissance Art

German Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Tillery L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-284, MDRST-284
📖 Description
This course explores the distinctive ways in which art was crafted and consumed in northern Europe during the age of Renaissance and Reformation. We will examine paintings and prints, propaganda and princely splendor, and carved altarpieces and ceremonial armor against the backdrop of both city and court, while considering issues of religious function, social use, and the economic history of the arts. The course also fosters a critical awareness of the methods of art history by drawing attention to scholarship on Northern art that has, in many ways, laid the foundations for modernity.

GOVT 201W-01: Introduction to Feminist Thought

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Marvin A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: WMGST-201

📖 Description

Topics include the history of feminist thought in Western culture, the broadening and complication of that canon to include examinations of race, class, gender, sexuality, ableism and ageism, and the implications of global feminist thought.

GOVT 206-01: Soft Power and the Global South

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Jumet K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
📖 Description
For decades, power in terms of foreign policy strategies was understood through the lens of hard power (e.g., coercive diplomacy & military intervention) to enforce national interests. Soft power, or the ability for states to shape the preferences of others through attractive power, is employed by states to influence how governments and populations in other countries perceive them. From educational exchanges to music and sports, this course examines soft power approaches employed by both large states and smaller ones mainly from the Global South. Through guest speakers, film, and in-class activities, the class will investigate how a country’s size and resources impact its soft power strategies and their effectiveness.

GOVT 218-01: Politics of Africa

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Pruett L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: AFRST-218
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-112 or GOVT-114
💬 Comments: (Comparative Politics)
📖 Description
Comparative examination of the domestic politics of sub-Saharan Africa. Central focus on explaining the recent rise of both multi-party democracy and state collapse across the continent. Examination of the colonial legacy, the nature of the African state, ethnic conflict, class divisions, the role of the military and the problems of economic underdevelopment.

GOVT 223-01: Political Parties and Ideologies

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Foy-Sutherland G
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-116
💬 Comments: By the end of this course, students will be conversant with the historical development of - and major scholarly debates over - American political parties and ideologies.
📖 Description
This course provides a basic overview of the major questions that have motivated academic research on political parties and ideologies in the United States for the past half-century. These questions include: why are parties formed? Do parties matter? How did conservatism and liberalism develop as distinct ideologies? How did they come to be adopted by the two major parties? And how do these parties' ideologies influence American politics? We will examine these questions through a combination of academic articles and books, news articles, and historical accounts.

We consider how to conduct transparent, rigorous, and evidence-based research, engage with statistical tools, and learn the basics of R.

GOVT 237-01: Russia and the World

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Rivera D
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: RSNST-237
📋 Prerequisites: Take any one of the following: GOVT-112, GOVT-114, one Russian Studies (RSNST) course, or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: (International Relations)
📖 Description
The course will examine Russia’s relations with both its post-Soviet neighbors and the West from the Tsarist era to the present. Topics to be covered include: the formation of the Russian Empire, the Cold War, the evolution of Russian-Western relations since the collapse of communism, Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, and the outbreak of a major war with Ukraine in 2022. A central theme of the course will be the evolution of Russian national identity, especially as it relates to Russia’s status as an empire and its relationship with the West.

GOVT 239-01: Digital Human Rights Investigations Project

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Rivera S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
🔀 Cross-listed: COLEG-239
📋 Prerequisites: A 100-level course in Government or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Research based on Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) is a technique pioneered by non-profit organizations and academic institutions to improve the transparency and fact-checking of investigative journalism and strengthen legal cases in the area of international human rights. This course provides students with an overview of these techniques and considers associated ethical, privacy, and technological concerns. Students will use techniques learned in class to gather and analyze OSINT materials related to international human rights violations in the context of the Russo-Ukrainian War. There is a required field trip to Washington, D.C., which involves staying overnight.

GOVT 240-01: International Security

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Pruett L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-114 or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: (International Relations)
📖 Description
This course examines the use of force to achieve political objectives by both state and non-state actors. It explores the origins, conduct, and outcomes of international and civil wars; the use of terrorism and other forms of violence against civilians; the motivations of people that participate in political violence; and the lasting effects of such participation. Includes both historical and contemporary cases, ranging from the First World War to the current conflict in Syria.

GOVT 241-01: Survey of Constitutional Law

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Anechiarico F
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-116 or a course in American History
💬 Comments: (American Politics)
📖 Description
Analysis of constitutional doctrines through major cases. Function of the Supreme Court as an instrument of government and arbiter of public policy. Doctrines include judicial review, federalism, interstate commerce, due process and questions of individual rights.

GOVT 249-01: American Political Thought

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Martin R
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-116, GOVT-117, GOVT-229, GOVT-241, GOVT-270, or consent of the instructor
💬 Comments: (Political Theory)
📖 Description
What does it mean to be an American? What are the principles of American politics? Considers the answers of Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, Alexis de Tocqueville, W.E.B. DuBois, Emma Goldman, John Dewey, Leo Strauss and William E. Connolly.

GOVT 273W-01: Justice Lab Seminar

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Sullivan H
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: PPOL-273
💬 Comments: Open to Justice Lab students only. This course forms part of the Justice Lab. Students must apply to be a part of the lab.
📖 Description
This seminar forms part of the justice lab program. It focuses on issues of politics and policy.

GOVT 281-01: Common Ground: A Laboratory for Civil Discourse

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Seidule T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: COLEG-281, HIST-281
💬 Comments: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
📖 Description
Common Ground will be a speaking intensive, history and government class where students learn about the history of free speech in America and on campus through practicums. While engaging with the history, students will learn to disagree, agreeably through different exercises focusing on the U.S. Constitution in a "Reacting to the Past" role-playing game, a LLM for the Founding Fathers, and free speech on campus issues, especially the 2005 Ward Churchill incident that roiled the Hamilton campus.

GOVT 285-01: Introduction to Environmental Politics

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Cannavo P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: ENVST-285
💬 Comments: Students will explore these topics directly and through selected policy issues, including forest politics, sprawl and climate change. (American Politics)
📖 Description
An overview of environmental politics, domestic and global. Topics include the environmental movement and its history and values, anti-environmentalism, environmental policy analysis, the relation between environmental science and politics, the domestic and international environmental policy processes, the North-South debate, globalization, race and environmental justice, and the implications of environmental politics for liberal democracy.

GOVT 291-01: International Political Economy

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Cafruny A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 5]
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-114
💬 Comments: (International Relations)
📖 Description
Examination of the development and evolution of the modern global economy and its political impact. Issues include global trade relations, the monetary system and international debt, the role of multinational corporations, foreign aid, imperialism and dependency, industrial competitiveness and the rise and impact of newly industrializing countries such as South Korea and Taiwan.

GOVT 305W-01: Native and Indigenous Political Thought

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Leonardo K
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One 200-level GOVT course in American politics, political theory, or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: (Political Theory)
📖 Description
This course investigates various texts in Native and Indigenous political thought. Themes may include indigeneity, colonialism, sovereignty, recognition, refusal, and resistance. Readings will center on the works of non-Western thinkers.

GOVT 315W-01: Foreign Policies of Middle Eastern States

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Jumet K
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-114
💬 Comments: (International Relations)
📖 Description
The Middle East is facing a period of instability and transformation. The aim of this course is to explore the foreign policy decisions of Middle Eastern states. Through class discussion, film, and guest speakers, this course will examine the security challenges facing major players in the region (Iran, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Turkey, Qatar, Egypt, Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon). Particular attention will be given to theories of foreign policy decision-making in nondemocratic states.

GOVT 316W-01: Civic Republicanism

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Cannavo P
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-117, ENVST-287, GOVT-287, or one course in American history.
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors, Juniors, & Sophomores (Political Theory)
📖 Description
Civic republicanism is a political tradition that emphasizes civic virtue, political participation, non-domination, and the common good. Civic republicanism influenced the American founding and the Abolitionist, labor, antipoverty, Civil Rights, feminist, and environmental movements. This course begins with the history of civic republicanism, including classic political thinkers like Aristotle, Wollstonecraft, Rousseau, Jefferson, Douglass, and Marx, and then explores contemporary republican political thought. Additionally, we look at how civic republicanism can inform responses to contemporary issues like racism, sexism, reproductive rights, homophobia, economic inequality, political corruption, threats to democracy, new technologies, and climate change.

GOVT 321-01: Term in Washington: Congressional and Executive Internships

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: TBA
👤 Instructor: De Bruin E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the concentration. Offered satisfactory/unsatisfactory only.
📖 Description
Twelve-week internships in relevant DC office. Interns assume some operational responsibility in the office and gain a perspective on the political and policy process in Washington DC. Does not count toward the concentration. Offered satisfactory/unsatisfactory only. Internship is subject to approval by DC Program Director. Klinkner (Fall); Cafruny (Spring). Taught in person, unless remote internships can be arranged.

GOVT 323-01: Term in Washington: Intern Participant-Observation

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: TBA
👤 Instructor: De Bruin E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the concentration.
📖 Description
Participants in the program are asked to evaluate their experience in government offices through a series of group discussions and papers focused on particular aspects of the internships.

GOVT 325-01: Term in Washington: Seminar

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: TBA
👤 Instructor: De Bruin E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
💬 Comments: (American Politics)
📖 Description
An academic seminar focusing on the public policy process and national issues.

GOVT 327-01: Term in Washington: Independent Research

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: TBA
👤 Instructor: De Bruin E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
💬 Comments: (American Politics)
📖 Description
Preparation and presentation of independent research on a problem related to public policy issues. Use of Washington’s unique human and data resources required.

GOVT 341W-01: Campaigns, Elections, and American Democracy

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Foy-Sutherland G
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-116
📖 Description
This course provides an overview of research on American campaigns and elections spanning the past half-century. We begin by examining elections in theory - focusing on research on electoral history, the role of political parties, and voter decision-making. The latter section of the course transitions to examining elections in practice - looking at research that analyzes key aspects of contemporary elections such as fundraising, campaign advertising, and voter mobilization.

GOVT 365W-01: Free Speech Theory

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Martin R
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: GOVT-229, GOVT-241, GOVT-270 or GOVT-276
💬 Comments: (Political Theory)
📖 Description
Analysis of competing theories of the liberty of expression in the American context. Focuses primarily on contemporary political and legal disputes over such morally divisive issues as "hate speech," campus speech codes, pornography, media and Internet censorship, and the proper role of free speech in a democracy. Examination of the evolution of American constitutional law concerning freedom of expression.

GOVT 366W-01: Chinese Foreign Policy

Government  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Chan A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: 200-level course in International Relations or Comparative Politics, or permission of instructor
💬 Comments: (Comparative Politics)
📖 Description
China’s ascendance as a global power has been dramatic. In this course, we will analyze the external and domestic determinants of Chinese foreign policy and the political, military, and economic implications of this shift in power for the rest of the world. We will examine what drives China’s interactions with other states,investigate competing sources of ideas and policy change, and engage in foreign policy analysis.

GOVT 419-01: Linowitz Seminar

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 6:30 PM – 9:30 PM
👤 Instructor: De Bruin E, Brindisi A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Permission of the department
💬 Comments: Instructor's Signature Required. Retakeable once, for a total of two instances, both counting toward the major. (International Relations) May be retaken for credit a maximum of two times. Different sections of this course may meet various International Relations, Comparative Politics, American Politics, or Political Theory requirements. See Government department or the applicable semester schedule for additional information.
📖 Description
The Sol M. Linowitz seminars are taught by governmental and policy practitioners who have occupied senior positions in government or with global non-government organizations (NGOs). They offer policy-oriented seminars for twelve Government and World Politics concentrators, who are enrolled through a competitive selection process. Professors may be senior diplomats or foreign service officers; state or federal elected officials; senior state or federal cabinet officers or administrative officials; or senior officials of foreign governments, international organizations, or important NGOs.

GOVT 550-01: Senior Project

Government  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Gorham A

📋 Prerequisites: One 300-level course in Government
💬 Comments: Instructor's Signature Req. Open to concentrators only

A senior project required for concentrators in the department who are not pursuing honors.

💬 Comments: Instructor's Signature Req. Open to concentrators only

GOVT 550-05: Senior Project
