GREEK 110-01: Elementary Ancient Greek

Greek  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Feltovich A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 3]
💬 Comments: Three class meetings a week, in addition to a drill session.
📖 Description
An introduction to the language and culture of Greece and the ancient Mediterranean. Thorough grounding in the grammar, syntax and vocabulary of ancient Greek. Reading and discussion of elementary passages from classical or New Testament Greek that cast light on ancient Mediterranean society and culture. For those with no previous knowledge of Greek.

GREEK 390-01: Topics in Ancient Greek Society and Culture

Greek  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Persad S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Any 200- or 300-level GREEK course
💬 Comments: May be retaken for credit.
📖 Description
Reading and discussion of original Greek texts that cast light on the history, society and culture of Greece and the ancient Mediterranean. Authors and topics vary.

HIST 107W-01: Borders and Borderlands in US History

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Esquivel N
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only
📖 Description
This course asks how territorial boundaries have evolved into a dispersed, interior regime of surveillance and control over the course of American history. Beginning with colonial-era treaties and other practices of boundary-making in early US history, we will turn to examine U.S.–Mexico borderlands as a region shaped not only by movement, exchange, and cultural intermingling, but also by the evolving power of the state and the contested processes of border‑making. Special emphasis will be given to the intertwined histories of Indigenous, Mexican, Black, Chinese, and Euro‑American communities and to examining how borders are produced, negotiated, and lived, while developing critical reading and writing skills in history.

HIST 109W-01: Early Modern Western Europe, 1450-1800

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Ambrose D
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📖 Description
Survey of transformation of Western Europe from the Renaissance through the French Revolution. Focuses on social, political, economic and intellectual developments; examination of primary sources and secondary studies. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

HIST 111-01: An Introduction to the History of the United States, 1861-2001.

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Esquivel N
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
📖 Description
Introduction to U.S. history and an overview of the Civil War and Reconstruction, the emergence of the U.S. as a global power, progressivism and the New Deal, the Cold War, the liberal and radical insurgencies of the 1960s, and the conservative revival of the 1970s to the present.

HIST 112W-01: The Black Power Movement

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Smith C
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📖 Description
The course will focus on the political history of the Black Power Movement. By 1966, Black Power advocates charged by Stokely Carmichael and the Black Panthers, began a series of meetings with the help of Black politicians like Adam Clayton Powell. By 1967 and 1968, these same activists began planning, holding, and developing rallies for a new U.S. constitutional convention. This class is a political and intellectual history on the legacy of the Black Power Movement, its organizations, leaders, and ideologies. The course seeks to uncover the intellectual history of Black Power as a movement for democratic practice and multiracial democracy in the United States.

HIST 115-01: Ancient Greek History and Culture

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: TBA
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: CLASC-115
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only
📖 Description
An introduction to the legacy of ancient Greece through the study of history, literature, philosophy, and art. This course will also consider the influence of neighboring cultures on Ancient Greece, including the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and the Persians, to name a few.

HIST 146W-01: Medieval Christianities

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Eldevik J
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: MDRST-146, RELST-146
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Sophomores, & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
A survey of the development of the Christian religion in premodern Eurasia and the Mediterranean, from its elevation to a state cult in the later Roman Empire to about 1450. Special consideration will be given to the growth of the church and processes of conversion, the problem of authority versus heresy and heterodoxy, and the relationship of the Christian churches to Islam and other non-Christian peoples. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

HIST 151W-01: A Global History of Oil

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Ren C
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ENVST-151
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs.
📖 Description
How was our current dependence on petroleum created, and how can historical thinking help us imagine a better future? This course combines approaches from environmental and social history to examine the oil industry from the 19th century to today. Students explore social and environmental justice movements, the lives of oil industry workers, and our changing global economy, emphasizing peoples and places that are often marginalized. Contribute to contemporary debates on fossil fuels by analyzing museum exhibits in a final writing project.

HIST 161W-01: Sages of the Tao in Chinese History

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Wilson T
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-161
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, and 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Examination of the two most significant sages in Chinese history and the disciples and schools that traced their origins to them. Close readings of texts attributed to Laozi and Confucius, the conflicting interpretations of their teachings throughout Chinese history, and the proliferation of schools that claimed to transmit their Tao. An eminent historian once said, “Every era has its own Confucius; it’s just that there are many different Confucius[es] in any one era.” This adage, as we shall see, applies to Laozi as well.

HIST 208W-01: Asian Temples in a Digital World

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Wilson T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-208, RELST-208
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Asian Studies, History, or Religious Studies
📖 Description
Examination of three aspects of Asian religions: temple as built space, ritual object (e.g., image, talisman, offering, etc.), and ritual practice as intentional use of objects and space. Students work in groups to research an Asian temple of their choice and curate a web-based exhibition of the history of and ritual practices conducted in their temple. Instruction in digital tools of collecting, analyzing, and representing materials in a web-based exhibition. Writing assignments include short essays and a final research project of the student’s design to be presented with text and images in digital form.

HIST 215-01: The American Civil War

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Isserman M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
Examines the causes, conduct and legacy of the American Civil War, with particular attention to the debate over slavery, the divergent social, economic and cultural development of the southern and northern states, the religious dimension of the war, battle front strategy and home front mobilization, the politics of emancipation, reconstruction, redemption and reconciliation, and the Civil War in popular memory down to the present.

HIST 222-01: Modern Russian History

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Keller S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: RSNST-222
📖 Description
An overview of Russian history from the emancipation of the serfs to the collapse of the Soviet Union. Themes of the course include how Russia and the USSR dealt with their sense of "backwardness" compared to Europe, the multi-national and multi-religious nature of this vast Eurasian state, and the meanings of "modernity."

HIST 223-01: Gender and Violence in the Middle Ages

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Eldevik J, Terrell K
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 8, So: 8, Jr: 8, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-223, MDRST-223
📋 Prerequisites: One 100-level course in literature or history, or AP 4 or 5 in English or history.
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only (History).
📖 Description
This course serves as an introduction to the field of Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Drawing on multiple disciplinary perspectives, including those of literature, law, history, and art, we will examine the intersection of ideas about the body, gender, and violence in the European Middle Ages. Readings may include the Bible and early patristic writings; the lives of saints; poems and advice manuals on courtly love; depictions of women in the Crusades; Icelandic sagas; and perspectives on the trial of Joan of Arc.

HIST 230-01: England, Ireland, Empire, 1485-1701

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Grant K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This course examines the shifting boundaries of sovereignty and religion in Britain and Ireland in the period from the founding of the Tudor monarchy to the Glorious Revolution. It simultaneously shows how England developed its power overseas through trade, colonization, and privateering. This course illuminates the disparate, multicultural societies over which the English monarchy extended its rule, demonstrating how tumultuous struggles to consolidate and sustain political authority in the ‘Atlantic archipelago’ corresponded with the global expansion of British commerce.

HIST 232-01: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Yaseen S
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-232, CNMS-232, MEIWS-232
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

HIST 254-01: Recent American History: The United States, 1941 to the Present

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Isserman M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
A survey of American political, economic, cultural and social life from the start of the Second World War to the present. Topics include the Second World War, the Cold War, McCarthyism, the Civil Rights Movement, the sixties and their aftermath, and the Reagan Revolution and its aftermath.

HIST 259-01: The Early Republic, 1800 to 1840: From Jefferson to Jackson

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Ambrose D
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
An intensive examination of the political, social, cultural, and economic history of the United States from the election of Jefferson to 1840. Focus on Jefferson's presidency, Lewis and Clark expedition, War of 1812, Second Great Awakening, slavery and its expansion, growth of antislavery and abolition, Indian removal, foreign relations, and the Market Revolution.

HIST 265-01: African-American Political History

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Smith C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This class is a survey of the role of African Americans in American electoral politics from Reconstruction to the 21st century and seeks to help students understand how Black people have navigated both mainstream and radical political ideologies to claim their citizenship in a multiracial democracy.

HIST 281-01: Common Ground: A Laboratory for Civil Discourse

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Seidule T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: COLEG-281, GOVT-281
💬 Comments: Open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only.
📖 Description
Common Ground will be a speaking intensive, history and government class where students learn about the history of free speech in America and on campus through practicums. While engaging with the history, students will learn to disagree, agreeably through different exercises focusing on the U.S. Constitution in a "Reacting to the Past" role-playing game, a LLM for the Founding Fathers, and free speech on campus issues, especially the 2005 Ward Churchill incident that roiled the Hamilton campus.

HIST 285-01: Modernity and Nationhood in China

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Wilson T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
Examination of the social and cultural forces contributing to the decline of imperial institutions beginning in the 19th century, as found in the Taiping Rebellion, cultural interaction with Western missionaries, traders, and military and nationalist revolutions in the 20th century. Readings and class discussions consider the coherence of nationhood in Chinese identity and reexamine the "Western impact" as a force in the formation of modernism in China.

HIST 288-01: The Corporation

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Ren C
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 4, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 4]
🔀 Cross-listed: ANTHR-288
📖 Description
The Corporation examines how corporations have evolved as economic, political, and cultural institutions, shaping and reflecting the societies in which they operate. Drawing on historical analysis and ethnographic perspectives, the course traces their development from early chartered companies to the 2008 financial crisis, exploring key transformations in corporate structure, legal personhood, and financialization. We will consider how corporations have been shaped by historical forces such as colonialism, industrialization, and neoliberalism, while also analyzing their cultural logics, organizational practices, and symbolic power. Readings will examine how corporations have reshaped labor, culture, and economic inequality, as well as the ways they have been challenged and reformed. By examining corporate influence across time and space, students will gain a deeper understanding of its role in the modern world.

HIST 289-01: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Advani A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-289, MDRST-289, MEIWS-289
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Fifty years ago, the scholar Marshall Hodgson coined the term "gunpowder empires" to describe the introduction of new military technology by early modern Islamic kingdoms across Eurasia, specifically in Turkey, Iran, and India. Using this cultural framework to study the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal Empires, this course will focus on issues of imperial power and expansion, social and religious authority, protest and dissent, language and literature, law and ethics, paintings and architecture, as well as gender and sexuality. We will explore the historiography of these Islamic polities along with reading primary sources including court chronicles, local histories, political treatises, religious texts, and poetry in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit, Hindavi and other languages.

HIST 296-01: Wonder and Certainty in Science and Religion

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Cooley M, Goodwillie C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: LTAM-296 MDRST-296
📖 Description
Are we the only rational beings in the universe? Is such a thing as a soul? Can we predict the future? The truism goes that history is told by the victors, and the same is true for the history of ideas -- so, join us for a journey into the history of ideas that haven't made it into modern textbooks. Featuring materials from Hamilton College’s Special Collections, this course focuses on a series of case studies from early modern Europe and the Atlantic world that represent pivot points to teleologies in the history of science and thought. The result is a history of wonderment followed by doubt, illuminating divergent and sometimes abandoned paths once frequented by the wisest among humankind.

HIST 297-01: Piety, Power, and Politics: Christianity in America, 1600-1890

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Ambrose D
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
Examination of Christianity in America from the era of European settlement to the end of the 19th century. Topics include encounters with Native American religions, revivalism, sectarianism, slavery and antislavery, religion and politics, theological developments, popular beliefs and practices, and the rise of unbelief.

HIST 340W-01: Topic: The Archive and Historians

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Yaseen S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
💬 Comments: Students in this course can opt-in for co-requisite archival research for an extra 0.5 course credit (HIST-183 History Workshop: Archival Practice and Theory).
📖 Description
This course examines how histories of borderlands and margins, emanating from empires and nationstates, turn them into simultaneous objects of desire and control. Through the example of Kashmir — long conceptualized as a famed paradisiacal land, which in the postcolonial era turned into a politically disputed and a heavily militarized zone — we will critically parse orientalist, nationalist, academic, and popular histories about such regions in South Asia and beyond. Building upon comparisons with similarly contested sites such as Palestine, the course will center a people’s understanding of history through counter historical narratives, literary works, protest music, and poetry.

HIST 365W-01: Arabs and Jews in the Middle East

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Keller S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: JWST-365, MEIWS-365
📋 Prerequisites: Any 200-level history course, GOVT-207, or permission of the instructor
📖 Description
Deep study of the Arab-Israeli conflict from the 1880s to the present. We will study the relations between Arab and Jewish communities, the roots of Zionism, Western imperialism, and Israeli and Palestinian social and political evolution.

HIST 367W-01: The History and Literature of Himalayan Mountaineering, from the 19th Century to the Present.

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Isserman M
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
💬 Comments: Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment.
📖 Description
Examines Himalayan mountaineering over the past 150 years, and its roots in imperial expansion, national rivalries, and cultural and social evolution. Topics include mountaineering in the age of empire, George Leigh-Mallory’s death on Everest, American mountaineering in the Himalaya, conquest of the 8,000 meter peaks, the role of Sherpas in mountaineering, and the rise of commercial mountaineering. (Writing-intensive.) There will be an optional 2-week field trip to the Annapurna region of Nepal over spring break, conditions permitting. Generous travel aid is available to make the trip affordable to all students in the course.

HIST 383W-01: Topics in British and Irish History: Photography in Britain and the Empire

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Grant K
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: one 200-level history course, or consent of the instructor.
📖 Description
This research seminar examines photographs as historical texts. It addresses changing photographic technologies and the many uses of photography in Britain and the Empire from visual art and scientific research to philanthropy and the categorization of criminals. Particular emphasis will be placed on photography’s role in representing and influencing ideas about class, race, and gender.

HIST 389-01: W.E.B. Du Bois and the Black Intellectual Tradition

History  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Smith C
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📖 Description
This course will center the work of sociologist W.E.B. Du Bois and the intellectual history of Black radical thinkers in the 19th and twentieth century of the United States of America. The class will engage students with Du Bois' seminal work, Black Reconstruction in America: 1860 - 1880. The course is designed to examine the history of Black intellectual thought and activism in the United States from 1865 through 2000. With Du Bois guiding the course, students will be introduced to a wide range of Black radical thinkers through American history. Students will analyze how Du Bois' political transformation throughout several decades reflects similar crises experienced by the nation’s Black intellectuals as they tried to recover and rebuild Reconstruction.

HIST 451W-01: Senior Seminar

History  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Grant K, Cooley M
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: HIST-450
💬 Comments: Open to Senior HIST Concentrators only.
📖 Description
This is part two of the senior project sequence. Students will research and write an article-length manuscript based on their proposal from HIST 450. Following the completion of thesis drafts, every student will participate in an oral defense of their thesis.

HSPST 120-01: Second Term Spanish

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Mesiti J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: HSPST-110 or placement
💬 Comments: Course meets MWF for 50 minutes plus a weekly TA session (50 minutes).
📖 Description
Second Term Spanish continues to build language skills and intercultural competence for students who have taken one semester of college-level Spanish (HSPST 110) or its equivalent previously. The course reviews basic grammatical concepts and introduces the more advanced ones, interweaving language study with cultural studies of the Spanish-speaking world. The course develops proficiency in speaking, listening, reading, and writing in Spanish with the goal of reaching intermediate level by the end of the semester.

HSPST 150-01: Fourth Term Spanish

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Sanchez Gumiel M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in HSPST-130 or HSPST-135, placement exam, or consent of instructor. Not open to students who have taken HSPST-140.
💬 Comments: Three hours of class weekly, with an additional weekly TA session. Taught in Spanish.
📖 Description
An advanced language course designed to strengthen and develop oral communication and writing skills. Conversation and debate play a central role and provide a framework for engaging with cultural topics and contemporary issues in the Spanish-speaking world. The course offers a rigorous review of Spanish grammar and seeks to refine students’ written expression through an array of formats including argumentative compositions, descriptive essays, creative narration, newspaper articles, and reviews.

HSPST 200W-01: Exploring Hispanic Texts

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Burke J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Grade of C+ or better in HSPST 150 or 151, placement or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Not Open to Those Who Took Hspst-201W Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. Taught in Spanish.
📖 Description
Introductory study of literature and culture from the Hispanic world (Spain, Latin America, and Hispanic United States), with an emphasis on refining oral and written skills in Spanish. Focus on written and oral argumentation, and textual analysis of various literary genres, including narrative, poetry, essay and drama. Additional cultural material studied includes film, art, music, and contemporary social issues. Advanced grammar in context and vocabulary building.

HSPST 210-01: Introductory Study of Spanish Literature

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Hernandez Zamora Y
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: HSPST-200 or consent of instructor

📖 Description
Intensive study and analysis of cultural concepts and selected literary works of Spain. Introduction to basic critical skills for literary and cultural analysis as applied to texts studied. Emphasis on oral performance, student participation and on original application of critical methodology in writing projects. The course includes a required one-day (Saturday) trip to New York City to see a Spanish performance.

HSPST 217-01: Introduction to U.S. Latinx Literatures

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Ambio M
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 7, Jr: 7, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-217, LTAM-217
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only Taught in English. Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Examines cultural production of representative U.S. Latinx writers primarily from the civil rights movement to present. The course explores Latinx writers’ engagement with language, political status, race, gender, nationality, and generational markers to reveal both the fluidity and instability of the Latinx imaginary. Readings include autobiographical and biographical works, bildungsroman, memoir, historical novel and vignettes in an exploration of the self and one’s relation to collective identity.

HSPST 223-01: Introduction to Hispanic Cinema

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Martinez Arias J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: HSPST 200W or HSPST 201W, or placement
💬 Comments: Taught in Spanish.
📖 Description
An introduction to film in the Hispanic world, exploring the development of different national traditions within Latin American and Spanish Cinema. At the same time, covers some of the basic tools for interpreting and writing about film. Editing, sound, cinematography and mise-en-scène are some of the key terms and concepts studied in order to understand how viewers and filmmakers create meaning in films. Particular attention to the interrelation of cinema and culture, and the intersection of aesthetics and politics.

HSPST 334-01: Transatlantic Surrealism

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Mesiti J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Taught in Spanish.
📖 Description
Dreams, the unconscious, and a 106,460,000 km² body of water we know as the Atlantic Ocean. Originally founded as a poetic movement in France, Surrealism quickly traveled across borders and creative disciplines, transforming beyond its revolutionary roots of the 1920s and 1930s. Using poetic thought, this course traces Hispanic Surrealism’s flux between Europe and Latin America, starting with its premodern predecessors before turning to its avant-garde rupture, and ending with its contemporary creators. Materials studied include poetry, cinema, and visual art.

HSPST 364-01: The Cinema of Icíar Bollaín

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Sanchez Gumiel M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Taught in Spanish.
📖 Description
Study of the work of Spanish filmmaker and actress Icíar Bollaín (Madrid, 1967), exploring a wide spectrum of cultural, historical, and sociopolitical themes related to contemporary Spain (1980s-today). From her directorial debut, Hola, ¿estás sola? (1995), these themes will be examined through films such as Te doy mis ojos (2002), También la lluvia (2010), El olivo (2016), and Maixabel (2021). Discussions will include feminism, gender violence, migration, cultural commodification, economic and job insecurity, colonialism, and the effects of the 2008 global financial crisis. Readings of historical and theoretical texts will support the analysis of Bollaín’s works in class.

HSPST 381-01: Indigeneity and Modernity in the Andes

Hispanic Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Martinez Arias J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in HSPST or SPAIN at the 200 level or above, or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: Taught in Spanish.
📖 Description
The cultural representations of religion, history, means of transportation, media, photography, etc., provide distinct points of view on how modernity has been perceived in the Andes. This course will introduce students to the recognition of those perspectives by looking closely at novels, short stories, and movies, produced from the 19th century to the present day. This course also will explore the diverse ways in which the intensification of modernity has changed the nature of Andean cultural production itself: its language, style, the narrator’s and characters’ worldviews, etc.

ITALN 230-01: Horror, Excess, Obscenity: Italy and its Specters

Italian  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Dani V
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
💬 Comments: Warning: This course will analyze materials that some may find unsettling and/or deeply disturbing. Course taught in English; no previous knowledge of Italian required.
📖 Description
Mainstream representations of Italian culture, art, and lifestyle often suggest that the country revolves around pleasure. Culinary richness, architectural wonders, passionate love, and lyrical masterpieces create an image of Italy that leaves little room for the menacing forces that still haunt it. By fully embracing a dialectical method that values contradictions and brings the repressed to the surface, this course explores what is horrific, excessive, and obscene in Italian culture. Through a theoretically informed inquiry, we will delve into the subsurface of deadly histories, censored literary objects, and extreme filmic experiments to examine not only the conditions that gave birth to them, but also the guises in which their specters continue to influence the present. By staring into the abyss of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, we will interrogate the politics of seeing what remains after catastrophe and whether aesthetic forms can—or cannot—represent the unthinkable. Myriads of old Gorgons await beneath the surface.

ITALN 301-01: Fuori di casa: Stories of Travels and Returns

Italian  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Cai C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: ITALN-200, ITALN-220, or approval of instructor.
💬 Comments: Taught in Italian.
📖 Description
This course explores the concept of "being away from home" through various representations of travels and returns in Italian literature, cinema, music, and art. In these stories of movements and border-crossing, we will reflect on the idea of "home" with shifting social and cultural perspectives across time in Italian culture from Dante to Ferrante. In their shared themes of home and belonging, exile and border-crossing, these stories will guide us in understanding Italy and Italian as we know today, while helping us find home in a culture and in a language that is not our own.

JLJS 101-01: Introduction to Law

Jurisprudence, Law, and Justice Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Eannace R
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: PPOL-101
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Years
📖 Description
Focus on the American system of law: principally constitutional law, criminal law, and the development of civil rights. Topics include philosophical approaches to justice, English common law, and comparative analysis of French civil law and legal codes in socialist political systems and in majority Muslim countries. Consideration of the challenges to trust in legal institutions from the Supreme Court to local courts and police. Attention also to legal regimes regarding refugees, Native Americans, and defendants with mental illness.

JWST 111W-01: Ancient Jewish Wisdom

Jewish Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: RELST-111
📖 Description
An introduction to the Jewish Tradition and Jewish way of reading.

JWST 261-01: Jewish Feminism

Jewish Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: RELST-261
📖 Description
This course examines the foundational texts, debates, and activism of Jewish feminism in the United States from the early 1970s to the present. Students will explore how Jewish women named and theorized gender inequality in Jewish law, ritual, theology, communal life, and cultural practice—and how those critiques reshaped American Judaism. Readings will situate Jewish feminist thought within wider developments in feminist, religious, and American social history. The course also considers LGBTQ Jewish ideas and activism, asking where they converge with, extend, or challenge Jewish feminist concerns. Students will gain a vocabulary for analyzing the movement’s central questions, historical evolution, and enduring impact on Jewish life today.

JWST 263-01: American Jewish Literature

Jewish Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: LIT-263, RELST-263
📖 Description
What makes a work “Jewish American literature”? Must it be written by a Jewish author, center Jewish characters or themes, or appear in a Jewish language? This course uses such questions to explore the American Jewish experience from the earliest Jewish settlement to the present, with particular attention to the period after 1865. Through fiction, poetry, memoir, drama, and other genres, students will examine how writers have represented migration, religion, family, race, belonging, assimilation, and cultural difference. Rather than imposing fixed definitions, the course treats “Jewish,” “American,” and “literature” as contested categories whose meanings have changed over time.

JWST 271-01: Israel Through Literature and Film

Jewish Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Brown-Sofer E
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
Analysis through Israeli Literature and Film of the internal and external conflicts that have shaped Israeli society since its founding as an independent state in 1948. The challenge of forging a national identity and identities out of diverse diasporas and cultures. Responses to repetitive trauma in an evolving Israeli identity. Readings and films engage students in moral, political, ideological and social debates and address the many sociopolitical, historical, and geographical conflicts of this small but ethnically, religiously, culturally and politically diverse society.

JWST 274-01: Building Jerusalem: The Making and Remaking of a Holy City

Jewish Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Van Loan T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-274, MEIWS-274
📖 Description
Since its foundation, the city of Jerusalem has been claimed materially and spiritually by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. This course will, through its art and architecture, trace the complex history of Jerusalem from ca. 957 BCE to today’s divided city. The art and architecture of the city is contextualized in a way that speaks beyond the often-used and simplistic tripartite manner of constructing identity and history in the city.

JWST 365W-01: Arabs and Jews in the Middle East

Jewish Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Keller S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-365, MEIWS-365
📋 Prerequisites: Any 200-level history course, GOVT-207, or permission of the instructor
📖 Description
Deep study of the Arab-Israeli conflict from the 1880s to the present. We will study the relations between Arab and Jewish communities, the roots of Zionism, Western imperialism, and Israeli and Palestinian social and political evolution.

LATIN 120-01: Elementary Latin II

Latin  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Weiner J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
💬 Comments: Three class meetings a week, in addition to a drill session. Language course not in English.
📖 Description
Continuation of LATIN-110. Further study of grammar, syntax and vocabulary, accompanied by reading and discussion of passages that cast light on the society and culture of ancient Rome and its empire. For students who have completed LATIN-110 or those who have had some Latin but require review.

LATIN 340-01: The Roman Hero

Latin  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Weiner J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Any 200- or 300-level LATIN course
📖 Description
Readings, in the original Latin, from Vergil’s Aeneid and other Roman epics. Consideration of the nature of heroism and epic poetry, with attention to the history, society and culture of the Roman world.

LIT 140W-01: Renaissance Outsiders

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Schillinger S
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to First Years only (History or Intermedia)
📖 Description
From artists to utopian dreamers to iconoclastic peasants, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries are teeming with marginalized people radically reimaging the terms of their own self-identity and rethinking the relationship between selfhood and the larger culture. As an interdisciplinary conversation, this course explores issues in literary, art and cultural history through the study of texts that expose and even help create a changing sense of selfhood in the early modern period.

LIT 146W-01: Black Women's Literary Renaissance

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Holman T
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: AFRST-146, WMGST-146
💬 Comments: Open to First Years and Sophomores only. Students are restricted to one 100-level writing-intensive LIT course. 100-level LIT courses may not be taken after 200-level LIT courses. (Intermedia or Theory) (SSIH)
📖 Description
The twenty-year period between 1970 and 1990 is often referred to as the “Black Women’s Literary Renaissance” due to the unprecedented amount of literary and cultural production from black women in the United States. This course explores its profound contributions to black life and literature. Students will examine the intersections and oppositions among political movements, such as the Lesbian Feminist Movement and the Black Power Movement, and identify how these connections shaped the aesthetic landscape of the time. Course materials will include essays, novels, poems, and visual art, featuring Alice Walker, Toni Cade Bambara, bell hooks, Lorna Simpson, and others.

LIT 153W-01: Literature: What Is It Good For?

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Taylor S
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to First-Years Only (FYC). Students are restricted to one 100-level writing-intensive LIT course. 100-level LIT courses may not be taken after 200-level LIT courses. (Genre or Theory)
📖 Description
Debates about the value of literature have long been tied to questions about its use. Literature has been praised—and condemned—as a source of pleasure, a medium for the transmission of knowledge, and a vehicle of personal expression. In order to determine why fiction matters, we will examine works that explore the power of literature to shape moral, social, and political realities, including philosophical manifestos, anti-slavery treatises, self-help manuals, and experimental novels. Works by Rousseau, Cugoano, Wollstonecraft, and George Eliot, as well as the film The Servant (1963).

LIT 155W-01: Rewriting Pocahontas, Rethinking American Literature

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:20 PM
👤 Instructor: Burdick C
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: (History or Intermedia) (SSIH)
📖 Description
Who was Pocahontas, and why are Americans still so obsessed with her? Where does Pocahontas the historical person end, and Pocahontas-the-myth begin? And how have Indigenous writers and scholars rewritten and rethought the Pocahontas narrative? In this course we will trace the historical development of “Pocahontas” across genres and media. Texts will include histories (John Smith’s Generall Historie), dramas (The Indian Princess, the first American play about American Indians), poems (Lydia Sigourney’s epic poem Pocahontas) and films (Disney’s Pocahontas and Malik’s The New World). We will read these settler-authored texts in conversation with Indigenous-authored accounts of the historical Pocahontas (Powhatan name Matoaka) and the Indian princess trope.

LIT 204W-01: Poetry and Poetics

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Yao S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: For first-years, one course in literature or a 4 or 5 on AP LIT or LANG. No prerequisite for upperclass students.
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. Not open to senior English or Creative Writing concentrators. (Genre or History) Not open to senior English or Creative Writing concentrators.
📖 Description
This course examines how poems work: how they are constructed, and how they produce meaning, pleasure, and cultural value. We will study poetry in terms of prosody, conventions, history, genre, and reception, with the goal of teaching the essential skills of close reading and contextual interpretation. Readings are primarily from the traditions of poetry written in English.

LIT 204W-02: Poetry and Poetics

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Burdick C
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: For first-years, one course in literature or a 4 or 5 on AP LIT or LANG. No prerequisite for upperclass students.
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. Not open to senior English or Creative Writing concentrators. (Genre or History) Not open to senior English or Creative Writing concentrators.
📖 Description
This course examines how poems work: how they are constructed, and how they produce meaning, pleasure, and cultural value. We will study poetry in terms of prosody, conventions, history, genre, and reception, with the goal of teaching the essential skills of close reading and contextual interpretation. Readings are primarily from the traditions of poetry written in English.

LIT 217-01: Introduction to U.S. Latinx Literatures

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Ambio M
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 7, Jr: 7, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: HSPST-217, LTAM-217
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only (Genre or History) Taught in English. Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Examines cultural production of representative U.S. Latinx writers primarily from the civil rights movement to present. The course explores Latinx writers’ engagement with language, political status, race, gender, nationality, and generational markers to reveal both the fluidity and instability of the Latinx imaginary. Readings include autobiographical and biographical works, bildungsroman, memoir, historical novel and vignettes in an exploration of the self and one’s relation to collective identity.

LIT 223-01: Gender and Violence in the Middle Ages

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Eldevik J, Terrell K
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 8, So: 8, Jr: 8, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-223, MDRST-223
📋 Prerequisites: One 100-level course in Literature or History or AP 4 or 5 in English or History
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only (History)
📖 Description
This course serves as an introduction to the field of Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Drawing on multiple disciplinary perspectives, including those of literature, law, history, and art, we will examine the intersection of ideas about the body, gender, and violence in the European Middle Ages. Readings may include the Bible and early patristic writings; the lives of saints; poems and advice manuals on courtly love; depictions of women in the Crusades; Icelandic sagas; and perspectives on the trial of Joan of Arc.

LIT 230-01: Bollywood Film

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Sundar P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-230
💬 Comments: (Genre or History) This course may be offered as writing-intensive or not writing-intensive, per the deparment. Refer to the schedule for details.
📖 Description
The course charts a history of Bollywood, India’s mainstream Hindi-language film industry. Although dismissed for its use of melodrama and song-dance sequences, Bollywood has long engaged with other global cinemas and critiqued social, cultural, and political trends. Readings and films span romances about gender and nation like Mother India (1957) and Chaudhvin Ka Chand (1960); the 1970s "angry young man" oeuvre and its later avatars, crime and terrorist films; diasporic family dramas like Kal Ho Naa Ho (2003); and crossover hits like The Lunch Box (2013) that address the globalized present.

LIT 232-01: Toni Morrison

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Holman T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
🔀 Cross-listed: AFRST-232
💬 Comments: (Theory or Genre)
📖 Description
This course is an in-depth study of Toni Morrison’s fictional works and critical writing. Students will explore her creative and scholarly contributions to ideas of community and genealogy, as well as to representations of race, gender, and nation. Students will also explore her attention to language, form, and literary theory. In studying both Morrison’s formal and theoretical commitments, students will develop an awareness of how literature serves as a vehicle for animating and critiquing social, historical, and ethical concerns in our world. Assignments will include short critical essays, collaborative presentations and projects, and readings will include "The Source of Self-Regard," "The Bluest Eye," "Song of Solomon," and "Jazz."

LIT 238W-01: The Films of the Coen Brothers: Genre and Pastiche at the end of the American Mythos

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM  |  Wed 7:00 PM – 10:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Schillinger S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-238
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Literature or Cinema and Media Studies, or permission of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. Instructor's signature required during schedule adjustment. (Intermedia or Theory)
📖 Description
This course will analyze the way the Coen Brothers’ films play with previously hegemonic myths about the American experience. How do their films negotiate expectations of genre? What happens to meaning when pastiche or appropriation become vital to the narrative and imaginary world of the films? We will watch up to a dozen films, including Fargo, No Country for Old Men, Miller’s Crossing, O Brother Where art Thou and The Big Lebowski, not quite in chronological order,. Readings from scholarly and theoretical material, as well as excerpts from many of their sources, from Homer to Hammett. We'll also consider some of the 20th century painting, architecture and style that informs their films. Mandatory out of class viewings.

LIT 255-01: Reconstituting the Constitution

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Widiss B
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Justice Lab. (History)
📖 Description
This course explores the “Constitutional Moment” as a broad sociocultural formation in the decades just before and after the turn of the nineteenth century, and as a recurring American phenomenon thereafter. We will begin by analyzing the founding documents as rhetorical performances, reading the aspirations and anxieties they express in relation to those legible in contemporaneous literary texts. Then we’ll turn to political, literary, and cinematic works across subsequent American generations that figuratively re-stage the founding moment even as they radically re-frame its stakes and stakeholders. Likely authors: A. Hamilton, T. Jefferson, W. Irving, H.D. Thoreau, F. Douglass, E.C. Stanton, W. Whitman, A. Lincoln, G. Stein, R. Ellison, G. Lucas, L.M. Miranda.

LIT 256-01: American Literature of the 19th Century

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Burdick C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: (Genre or History)
📖 Description
A lot happened in this country in the nineteenth century. Slavery was expanded and then eventually abolished. Women fought for equal rights and didn't get them. Indigenous peoples were attacked and displaced – but refused to vanish. Waves of immigrants arrived and dispersed. There was a civil war. Meanwhile, the novel became a mass-market media sensation. Poetry was a set of popular genres that everyone read. Melodramas attracted large crowds. New versions of American philosophy rose and fell. People tried to write their life stories. In this course we will read some of those novels, poems, autobiographies, and philosophical essays (by Stowe, Wheatley, Douglass, Thoreau, and Whitman, among others) against the historical backdrop of war, immigration, forced removal, misogyny, and racism.

LIT 262-01: Siberian Text

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Abrahamyan A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: AIIS-262, RSNST-262
📖 Description
This course is an exploration of five centuries of writing in and about Siberia. While we will root ourselves in the socio-historical context, our main goal is to engage meaningfully with the very process of the formation of the Siberian Text. By this, scholars of the region mean the body of works that emerged out of the geographical, political, anthropological, and cultural categorizations of Siberia. The plurality of voices and the diversity of spatial experiences engaged in the process of creating the Siberian Text include travelers, criminals, political prisoners, religious dissenters, shamans, hunters, ethnographers, missionaries, vagabonds, and peasants. Probing the fraught legacy of the current spatial discourse on Siberia, the course will examine a variety of media and genres, including official documents, travelogues, oral tradition(s), works of fiction, autobiographies, pictorial art, and film. In addition to the transnational and transhistorical dimensions, we will engage with theories of space and place, imagined geographies, and ecocriticism.

LIT 263-01: American Jewish Literature

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: JWST-263, RELST-263
📖 Description
What makes a work “Jewish American literature”? Must it be written by a Jewish author, center Jewish characters or themes, or appear in a Jewish language? This course uses such questions to explore the American Jewish experience from the earliest Jewish settlement to the present, with particular attention to the period after 1865. Through fiction, poetry, memoir, drama, and other genres, students will examine how writers have represented migration, religion, family, race, belonging, assimilation, and cultural difference. Rather than imposing fixed definitions, the course treats “Jewish,” “American,” and “literature” as contested categories whose meanings have changed over time.

LIT 289-02: Video Essays: Writing with Sound and Image

Literature  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Sundar P
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-289
💬 Comments: 0.5 credit course; Meets 1/20/27-3/12/27 Open to Sophomores, Juniors, and Seniors.
📖 Description
Videographic criticism is a multimodal form of writing. In using sound and image to comment on audiovisual texts, the video essay blurs the line between object and method of study. This hands-on humanities lab introduces students to a wide range of videographic techniques and formats, and some of the theoretical and philosophical concerns driving recent developments in the field. Students learn to not only craft their own video essays, but display greater reflexivity about their aesthetic choices, interventions and compositional process. No prior editing or other digital experience required.

LIT 301-01: Avant Garde: Cinema as Theory and Critique

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 7:00 PM – 10:00 PM
👤 Instructor: MacDonald S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-301, CNMS-301
💬 Comments: Not open to first-year students.
📖 Description
A history of alternatives to commercial movies, focusing on surrealist and dadaist film, visual music, psychodrama, direct cinema, the film society movement, personal cinema, the New American Cinema, structuralism, Queer cinema, feminist cinema, minor cinema, recycled cinema and devotional cinema. While conventional entertainment films use the novel, the short story and the stage drama as their primary instigations, experimental and avant-garde films are analogous to music, poetry, painting, sculpture and collage.

LIT 344W-01: 'earing Accent --Methods

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: TBA
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: A 200-level course in Literature, Africana Studies, or Women's and Gender Studies
💬 Comments: (Intermedia) (Methods)
📖 Description
Everyone speaks with an accent. But where some people's speech is deemed "neutral," others are cast as "accented." Racialized and classed perceptions about language and fluency infuse literature as well as the realms of education, housing, employment, and immigration. How might we reframe "accent" such that it unsettles assumptions about linguistic identity and cultural worth? To what extent are accents visual, aural, and textual, not just oral? Course texts may include: My Fair Lady; Sorry to Bother You; episodes from The Simpsons and Modern Family; creative non-fiction, fiction, and poetry.

LIT 347W-01: Shakespeare and Appropriation

Literature  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Schillinger S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores (Genre or History)
📖 Description
This class focuses on appropriation as a central condition for considering Shakespeare's drama. Along with plays by Shakespeare we will study how his plays have been appropriated by others. In addition, we will investigate how Shakespeare considered appropriation and adaptation a prime method of literary production by studying contemporary plays, ancient literature and a diversity other sources that Shakespeare likely considered in his own composition process. In so doing we will see the exchanges and vital engagement Shakespeare shows with his own reading.

LIT 353-01: Origins of the Now: Transatlantic Modernism--Methods

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Yao S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One 200-level course in Literature
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores (Methods)
📖 Description
This course explores the origin stories of several literary and cultural forms that we now take for granted, including free verse, film, the literary magazine, and stream-of-consciousness narration. To do so, we will look at how early 20th century American and British writers and artists worked to reconceive foundational notions such as class, race, gender, self, sex, and time in response to the collapse of traditional Victorian values. Readings and viewings include works by Chaplin, Eliot, H.D., Griffith, Hughes, Joyce, Larsen, Loy, Pound, Toomer, Woolf and other possibilities. Attention given to the various scholarly methods for studying this rich and diverse literature.

LIT 356-01: Women and the Enlightenment

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Taylor S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: A 200-level course in Literature
💬 Comments: (History or Theory)
📖 Description
This course explores women’s relation to the intellectual and political culture of Enlightenment Britain. We will study how warring ideas about the rights of man shaped conceptions and representations of sexual difference and womanhood over the course of the long eighteenth century. Treating "woman" as a historical category will, in turn, help us to better understand the underlying assumptions and consequences of our own thinking about gender. Primary texts by Mary Astell, Mary Wollstonecraft, Austen, and Mme de Stael. Feminist scholarship by Nancy K. Miller, Nancy Armstrong, and Toril Moi.

LIT 439-01: Race and Nation in the Middle Ages

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Terrell K
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in Literature
💬 Comments: (History)
📖 Description
What did race and nation mean in the Middle Ages? We’ll first examine English attempts to establish a unified national identity out of a history of invasion and colonization. We’ll consider the role of Jews in England, as well as examples of Celtic resistance to English imperialism. Then we’ll turn to writing that explores English identity in an international context, to see how real and imagined contact with other cultures—particularly during the Crusades—influences conceptions of nation, race, and identity. Genres include travel writing, drama, romance, and historical narrative.

LIT 465-01: Faulkner and the South

Literature  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Widiss B
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in Literature
💬 Comments: (Genre or History)
📖 Description
Faulkner’s major novels, published between the late 1920s and the early 1940s, trace his most impassioned struggle with the legacies of slavery, the enduring hierarchies of gender and class, and the rising specter of industrialization’s destructive force. We’ll explore the series of radical formal innovations Faulkner arrived at in order to convey these stories, and to convey the inextricability of one from the next—both in American society and in individual consciousness. Readings: Light in August, Absalom, Absalom, Go Down, Moses, and more.

LIT 497-01: Seminar: Independent Projects

Literature  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Taylor S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Permission of the department
💬 Comments: Instructor's Signature Req. Graded Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory
📖 Description
In this seminar, students will pursue independent research projects culminating in a longer paper (25-35 pages) on a topic of their choosing. Seminar sessions will discuss strategies for organizing and drafting a longer paper, time management, the best ways to use research tools, and different ideas about how to revise; later there will be opportunities to share drafts and address issues that arise.

LTAM 165-01: Latin American Music

Latin American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Badue A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: MUSIC-165/265
📖 Description
Through the lens of musicology and ethnomusicology, this course explores folk/vernacular, popular, and classical music from various Latin American locales and Latino societies in the U.S. Lessons and readings include genres, instruments, and performance practices as well as contextualization with history, politics, and entertainment. Course also interrogates what defines Latin American and Latino musical identities. The course includes in-class, hands-on performances. No ability to read music is required.

LTAM 217-01: Introduction to U.S. Latinx Literatures

Latin American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Ambio M
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 7, Jr: 7, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: HSPST-217, LIT-217
💬 Comments: Taught in English. Not open to seniors.
📖 Description
Examines cultural production of representative U.S. Latinx writers primarily from the civil rights movement to present. The course explores Latinx writers’ engagement with language, political status, race, gender, nationality, and generational markers to reveal both the fluidity and instability of the Latinx imaginary. Readings include autobiographical and biographical works, bildungsroman, memoir, historical novel and vignettes in an exploration of the self and one’s relation to collective identity.

LTAM 265-01: Latin American Music

Latin American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Badue A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: MUSIC-165/265
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Sophomores, & 1st Yrs. Open to Music majors/minors only or instructor permission.

Through the lens of musicology and ethnomusicology, this course explores folk/vernacular, popular, and classical music from various Latin American locales and Latino societies in the U.S. Lessons and readings include genres, instruments, and performance practices as well as contextualization with history, politics, and entertainment. Course also interrogates what defines Latin American and Latino musical identities. The course includes in-class, hands-on performances. No ability to read music is required.

LTAM 296-01: Wonder and Certainty in Science and Religion

Latin American Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Cooley M, Goodwillie C

💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Are we the only rational beings in the universe? Is such a thing as a soul? Can we predict the future? The truism goes that history is told by the victors, and the same is true for the history of ideas -- so, join us for a journey into the history of ideas that haven't made it into modern textbooks. Featuring materials from Hamilton College’s Special Collections, this course focuses on a series of case studies from early modern Europe and the Atlantic world that represent pivot points to teleologies in the history of science and thought. The result is a history of wonderment followed by doubt, illuminating divergent and sometimes abandoned paths once frequented by the wisest among humankind.

MATH 260-01: Decisions by Design: Applied Mathematics in Society

Mathematics and Statistics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Gibbons C
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: MATH-116 and MATH-224
📖 Description
This course introduces applied mathematics in various social contexts with an emphasis on communication to non-experts. Its focus is exploring how mathematical tools such as calculus, linear algebra, optimization, and algorithms help shape decision-making in real-world applications. Depending on instructor expertise and student interest, applications may include search algorithms, apportionment methods, resource allocation, political districting, and more. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with mathematical skills to analyze complex systems and think critically about how to deploy mathematics to solve real-world problems.

MATH 356-01: Statistical Methods in Machine Learning

🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM

📖 Description

Group theory is used in many areas of mathematics and other STEM fields. This course will explore the basic structures and properties of groups as well as some basic operations on groups. The theory will be introduced and illustrated through classic examples. Applications of groups will also be discussed.

MDRST 146W-01: Medieval Christianities

Medieval and Renaissance Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Eldevik J
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-146, RELST-146
📖 Description
A survey of the development of the Christian religion in premodern Eurasia and the Mediterranean, from its elevation to a state cult in the later Roman Empire to about 1450. Special consideration will be given to the growth of the church and processes of conversion, the problem of authority versus heresy and heterodoxy, and the relationship of the Christian churches to Islam and other non-Christian peoples. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

MDRST 223-01: Gender and Violence in the Middle Ages

Medieval and Renaissance Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 9:00 AM – 9:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Eldevik J, Terrell K
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats [Fr: 8, So: 8, Jr: 8, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-223 / LIT-223
📋 Prerequisites: One 100-level course in Literature (LIT) or History (HIST), or AP 4 or 5 in English or History
💬 Comments: (History)
📖 Description
This course serves as an introduction to the field of Medieval and Renaissance Studies. Drawing on multiple disciplinary perspectives, including those of literature, law, history, and art, we will examine the intersection of ideas about the body, gender, and violence in the European Middle Ages. Readings may include the Bible and early patristic writings; the lives of saints; poems and advice manuals on courtly love; depictions of women in the Crusades; Icelandic sagas; and perspectives on the trial of Joan of Arc.

MDRST 284-01: Northern Renaissance Art

Medieval and Renaissance Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Tillery L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-284 / GERMN-284
📖 Description
This course explores the distinctive ways in which art was crafted and consumed in northern Europe during the age of Renaissance and Reformation. We will examine paintings and prints, propaganda and princely splendor, and carved altarpieces and ceremonial armor against the backdrop of both city and court, while considering issues of religious function, social use, and the economic history of the arts. The course also fosters a critical awareness of the methods of art history by drawing attention to scholarship on Northern art that has, in many ways, laid the foundations for modernity.

MDRST 289-01: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800

Medieval and Renaissance Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Advani A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-289, HIST-289, MEIWS-289
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs
📖 Description
Fifty years ago, the scholar Marshall Hodgson coined the term "gunpowder empires" to describe the introduction of new military technology by early modern Islamic kingdoms across Eurasia, specifically in Turkey, Iran, and India. Using this cultural framework to study the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal Empires, this course will focus on issues of imperial power and expansion, social and religious authority, protest and dissent, language and literature, law and ethics, paintings and architecture, as well as gender and sexuality. We will explore the historiography of these Islamic polities along with reading primary sources including court chronicles, local histories, political treatises, religious texts, and poetry in Turkish, Arabic, Persian, Sanskrit, Hindavi and other languages.

MDRST 296-01: Wonder and Certainty in Science and Religion

Medieval and Renaissance Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Cooley M, Goodwillie C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-296 LTAM-296
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Are we the only rational beings in the universe? Is such a thing as a soul? Can we predict the future? The truism goes that history is told by the victors, and the same is true for the history of ideas -- so, join us for a journey into the history of ideas that haven't made it into modern textbooks. Featuring materials from Hamilton College’s Special Collections, this course focuses on a series of case studies from early modern Europe and the Atlantic world that represent pivot points to teleologies in the history of science and thought. The result is a history of wonderment followed by doubt, illuminating divergent and sometimes abandoned paths once frequented by the wisest among humankind.

MDRST 346W-01: Madness, Lovesickness, and Jinns

Medieval and Renaissance Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Advani A
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-346, MEIWS-346
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Sophomores. First Years require instructor permission.
📖 Description
“Madness” evokes images of rambling, potentially violent, individuals on the margins of society. How did historical attitudes to insanity evolve in early modern and modern Eurasia? Were madpeople always ostracized or were they simply objects of sympathy and pity? What did hospitals and other networks of care and healing look like for mentally ill patients? In poetry, the pain of separation of the lover from their beloved produced lovesickness. Finally, demonic possession of the brain by jinns (Islamic spirits) was thought to cause madness. How can we understand the literary, religious and supernatural world of these actors without dismissing it? This course will take a holistic view of insanity while engaging with the rise of asylums or other lunatic institutions.

MEIWS 210-01: Minorities in the Middle East: History, Religion, and Relations with Political Powers

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Amir S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARABC-210, RELST-210
📖 Description
This course explores how minority communities in the Middle East—Druze, ʿAlawites, Kurds, Yezidis, Armenians, Maronites, Copts, Assyrians, and others—have been formed and transformed from the late Ottoman era to the present. Beginning with the shift from imperial pluralism to nation-state “minorities,” it examines how religion, identity, nationalism, and political power shape communal identity and minority–state relations. Case studies span Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, addressing genocide, displacement, nationalism, citizenship, security, and diaspora. Drawing on history, anthropology, religious studies, and political science, students examine how communities negotiate identity, power, and recognition in a plural Middle East. This course examines historical and contemporary experiences of minority communities in the Middle East. Some course materials address difficult subjects, including genocide, mass violence, persecution, forced displacement, sexual violence, religious and ethnic discrimination, and war. These topics are approached in their historical and scholarly contexts and are essential to understanding the experiences of the communities studied in the course.

MEIWS 232-01: Costs of Resistance: History Through Film

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Yaseen S
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-232, CNMS-232, HIST-232
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Through films and documentaries about places with contentious histories and ongoing political conflicts, this course will examine the solidarities and fractures that resistance against colonial and foreign control brings about in struggling societies. The course will particularly explore the anticolonial struggles of Palestinians, Algerians, Irish, Kurds, Kashmiris, Tamils, and Indigenous Americans, among others, and in doing so engage with themes of sovereignty and self-determination, nationality and belonging, and history and memory. Such inquiries not only have real-world stakes for peoples' survival and political identities, but also shape in profound ways the imaginations and practices of resistance and solidarity across the globe.

MEIWS 274-01: Building Jerusalem: The Making and Remaking of a Holy City

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Van Loan T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-274, JWST-274
📖 Description
Since its foundation, the city of Jerusalem has been claimed materially and spiritually by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. This course will, through its art and architecture, trace the complex history of Jerusalem from ca. 957 BCE to today’s divided city. The art and architecture of the city is contextualized in a way that speaks beyond the often-used and simplistic tripartite manner of constructing identity and history in the city.

MEIWS 289-01: Gunpowder Islam: Empires in Turkey, Iran, and India, c.1500-1800

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Advani A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-289, HIST-289, MDRST-289
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs

MEIWS 315-01: Advanced Arabic

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 12:00 PM – 12:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Koukjian M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARABC-315
📋 Prerequisites: ARABC-115, ARABC-116, ARABC-215, and ARABC-216 or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: This course is sponsored by the New York Six Liberal Arts Consortium, from an award by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation.
📖 Description
Advanced Arabic is a course designed for students who have completed four semesters of Arabic. The course will help students move from Intermediate Middle level to Advanced. Students will focus on acquiring more vocabulary and more knowledge of the fundamental grammatical and morphological structures of the language. They will also learn about the literary traditions of the Arab World through readings of abridged literary works. The instructor will select the literary work and prepare all the material used for the class.

MEIWS 345-01: Postcolonial Theory and Islamic Art

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Van Loan T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARTH-345
📖 Description
How does the study of art and architectural history interface with colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial structures of power? This is a pressing question for those who study the visual cultures of the Middle East, a region in which these power structures have had considerable impact historically as well as in the contemporary moment. This class will consider from theoretical and practical vantage points how colonial, postcolonial, and neocolonial systems and institutions have governed or influenced the methods of study, scope, and modes of display of historical art from the Middle East. Topics will include colonial-era collection and museum practices, Orientalism and its critics, post-colonial nationalist art historical discourses, cultural heritage in and during the ‘wars on terror’, and visual discourses of contemporary Islamophobia. Students may pursue research projects with objects or items from the Wellin Museum and/or the Michael Lang ’67 Special Collections and Archives.

MEIWS 346W-01: Madness, Lovesickness, and Jinns
