MEIWS 365W-01: Arabs and Jews in the Middle East

Middle East and Islamic World Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Keller S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-365, JWST-365
📋 Prerequisites: Any 200-level history course, GOVT-207, or permission of the instructor
📖 Description
Deep study of the Arab-Israeli conflict from the 1880s to the present. We will study the relations between Arab and Jewish communities, the roots of Zionism, Western imperialism, and Israeli and Palestinian social and political evolution.

MUSIC 110-01: Introduction to Music Theory

Theory and Composition  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Botha C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs Students who can already read music in both treble and bass clefs, and have a basic knowledge of (1) key and meter signatures, (2) major and minor scales, and (3) simple rhythms should instead register for MUSIC-210.
📖 Description
An introductory survey of the most important aspects of Western music theory necessary for performing, interpreting, and composing music. Topics range from reading notes and rhythms to analyzing and formulating chord progressions. Study of basic musical structures of the Western classical tonal idiom ("classical" music) and contemporary popular music practices that have developed from that. No previous knowledge of music required.

MUSIC 113-01: Introduction to Media: Integrated Media and Emerging Practices

Music  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Fri 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 143  |  Fri 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 124
👤 Instructor: Huff A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 6, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 2]
🔀 Cross-listed: ART-113 DARTS-113
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph, Jrs, and Srs
📖 Description
This course will serve as an introduction to digital technology in contemporary art making as it relates to interactivity, collaboration, and emerging practices. Emphasis will be placed on hands on experimentation and exploration across disciplines. We will cover installation art, web art, digital and time-based art, and immersive environments. Students will gain an overview of emerging digital practices, collaborative production strategies and correlations to social, aesthetic and theoretical issues. Other topics may include virtuality, performance, cyborgs, and network culture.

MUSIC 117-01: Roots Music to Country Music: The Making of an American Sound

Literature and History of Music  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Hamessley L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]

💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Yrs No previous knowledge of music required. Music concentrators and minors are strongly encouraged to register for MUSIC-217. MUSIC-217 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 200-level only with instructor’s permission.
📖 Description
Study of country music from its roots in cowboy songs, fiddle tunes, blues, bluegrass, and gospel hymns to current artists like The [Dixie] Chicks, Taylor Swift, and Brad Paisley. Artists include the Carter Family, Hank Williams, Patsy Cline, Dolly Parton, Willie Nelson, Emmylou Harris, Lynyrd Skynyrd, & Garth Brooks. Study of the musical elements, social class, gender roles, and cultural contexts of styles such as Western Swing, Honky-Tonk, Rockabilly, the Nashville Sound, Southern Rock, and Alt-country. Includes films such as Coal Miner's Daughter, Nashville, and O Brother, Where Art Thou?

MUSIC 165-01: Latin American Music

🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Badue A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: LTAM-165/265
📖 Description
Through the lens of musicology and ethnomusicology, this course explores folk/vernacular, popular, and classical music from various Latin American locales and Latino societies in the U.S. Lessons and readings include genres, instruments, and performance practices as well as contextualization with history, politics, and entertainment. Course also interrogates what defines Latin American and Latino musical identities. The course includes in-class, hands-on performances. No ability to read music is required.

MUSIC 221-01: From Bach to Bartok

Literature and History of Music  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ LIST 106
👤 Instructor: Badue A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: MUSIC-100, MUSIC-110, MUSIC-210, MUSIC-211, MUSIC-220, MUSIC-141/142, or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Instrumental music from the eighteenth, nineteenth, and first half of the twentieth centuries with an emphasis on orchestral works by composers such as Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Brahms, Mahler, Debussy, Stravinsky, and Bartók. Attention also given to piano and chamber works, including music by women composers. Consideration of the history and development of musical instruments and the use of instrumental classical music in popular culture (as in the films Apocalypse Now, The Shining, 2001: A Space Odyssey, Platoon).

MUSIC 231-01: Intermediate Media: New Frontiers in Storytelling

Music  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 143  |  Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 124
👤 Instructor: Huff A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: DARTS-231, THETR-231
📋 Prerequisites: Any intro-level Digital Arts studio course, including cross-listed.
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab
📖 Description
This class will survey and create emergent and non -linear forms of storytelling using digital and hybrid tools. We will examine notions of narrative authority and hybridity in a digital age and think through different ways we might use technology to distill, break apart or reify modes of communication and visual metaphor. Discussion will push boundaries of traditional storytelling and consider connectivity, liveness and embodied presence. This course will draw on multiple forms of expression including but not limited to digital media, performance, sound, XR, web, and network environments.

MUSIC 245-01: Music in American Film

Literature and History of Music  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ LIST 106  |  Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KRJH 125
👤 Instructor: Hamessley L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: AMST-245/345
📋 Prerequisites: Two courses, in any combination, in MUSIC, Cinema and Media Studies (CNMS), or Literature (LIT)
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Years Three hours per week for film viewings in addition to class time. Music 345 has an additional independent project. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor’s permission.
📖 Description
Examination of music in American film from silent films to the present with emphasis on the golden age of Hollywood. Topics include the development of musical conventions in film, different approaches of film composers (Steiner, Tiomkin, Rózsa, Herrmann, Newman, Bernstein, Williams), the meanings that music brings to film narratives. Includes films such as Casablanca, The Adventures of Robin Hood, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, A Streetcar Named Desire, Amadeus, The Shawshank Redemption, Oh Brother, Where Art Thou? Special attention to Hitchcock films (Psycho, Vertigo, Rear Window).

MUSIC 267-01: Jazz Connections

Literature and History of Music  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ SCHA 108
👤 Instructor: Condon G
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: AFRST-267/367
📋 Prerequisites: MUSIC 161/261, AFRST 161/261, MUSIC 257/357, AFRST 257/357, or consent instructor
💬 Comments: Not open to students who have taken MUSIC/AFRST 259/359. Registration at the 300-level only with instructor's permission.
📖 Description
An advanced jazz course that builds on the topics covered in Jazz Foundations (MUSIC 161), and examines the construction of the “jazz tradition” from a historiographical perspective. Considers how the development of jazz, and its construction in the context of educational institutions, both reflects and shapes concepts of race and gender in American culture. Includes an examination of the impact of jazz genres including hip hop, R&B, and gospel, and focuses on the international proliferation of jazz.

MUSIC 270-01: Introduction to Music, Sound, and Technology

Theory and Composition  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM @ KTSA 143
👤 Instructor: Carter R
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📖 Description
An introduction to the essential tools of 21st-century musicians, with an emphasis on creative practice and critical reflection. Students will learn to record, edit, process, and synthesize sound digitally; produce music using MIDI keyboards and software instruments; distribute their work; and critically engage with topics linked to the emergence of digital audio technologies. Listening and reading will include a wide range of works by Halim El-Dabh, Karlheinz Stockhausen, Pauline Oliveros, Pamela Z, and others. Open to all students regardless of musical background; additional resources for relevant music theory will be provided.

Neuroscience  •  1 Credit

NEURO 204-01: Fundamentals of Human Neuroscience

Neuroscience  •  1 Credit

NEURO 211-01: Genes, Molecules, and Cells

Neuroscience  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Datta R
👥 Capacity: 30 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: BIO-211
📋 Prerequisites: Any BIO-100
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores only. Not open to those who took BIO 248. Freshman and sophomores only; juniors and seniors will need permission of instructor.
📖 Description
An intermediate course that examines genetics and biochemistry within the context of the cell. This course will focus on the macromolecules of life, genetic material and classical genetics, fundamental biochemical pathways, and cellular structure and function. A particular focus will be placed on proteins and nucleic acids and how cells use these molecules to direct the mechanisms of inheritance, energy production, and cellular reproduction. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.
🔬 Required Co-requisite Lab Sections (2 available):
NEURO 211L-1
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM–4:00 PM @ SCCT 2089 | 👤 Instructor: Relles N | 👥 Seats: 20
NEURO 211L-2
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM–4:00 PM @ SCCT 2089 | 👤 Instructor: Relles N | 👥 Seats: 20

NEURO 305-01: Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias

Neuroscience  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Yeung L
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: BIO-205, NEURO-205, or PSYCH-205
📖 Description
Dementia involves progressive loss of cognitive functions, associated with unique patterns of neurodegeneration in the brain. For example, Alzheimer’s disease is associated with memory loss and temporal lobe atrophy, whereas frontotemporal dementia is characterized by behavioral changes associated with frontal lobe atrophy. This course will discuss the different etiologies of dementia, the biological changes associated with different subtypes, risk factors (behavioral, genetic, etc.), neuropsychological and imaging-based methods for diagnosis, current treatment options, and the emotional, social, and economic costs of dementia on patients and caregivers. We will delve into primary scientific literature covering current theories and findings, and will explore cultural depictions to better understand dementia from multiple viewpoints. This course has substantial neurobiology content and students are required to have completed Fundamentals of Neurobiology (Neuro 205) to enroll.

NEURO 329-01: Stress and Psychophysiology

Neuroscience  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM  |  Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Faig K
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: PSYCH-329
📋 Prerequisites: Psych/Neuro 201 and Psych/Neuro 204 or 205
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology. (Same as PSYCH/NEURO-329.)
📖 Description
A theoretical and methodological exploration of the psychological and physiological mechanisms of stress. Questions will include: How does psychological stress impact health and well-being? What neurobiological mechanisms are involved? What is the role of environmental context? Laboratory exercises will include designing original experiments to examine the role of stress on behavior and physiological activity, as well as analyzing data, writing papers based on findings, and oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

📖 Description
The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

PHIL 115W-01: Existentialism

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 8:00 AM – 8:50 AM

📖 Description

PHIL 117W-01: Introduction to Political Theory

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM

PHIL 117W-02: Introduction to Political Theory

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Gorham A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats

📖 Description

PHIL 120-01: Philosophical Perspectives on the Self

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 10:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Janack M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to First Years and Sophomores only Open to first years and sophomores in the spring; open only to first years in the fall.
📖 Description
What is a self? Does each person have one? Does each person have only one? How is the self related to the soul? Is it unchanging or in constant flux? What is the relationship between the self and the body? Examination of personal identity, the self and the soul as these topics are addressed in traditional philosophical texts, literature and the natural and behavioral sciences.

PHIL 132W-01: Evil, Distraction, and How to Build a Better World

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Amico-Korby D
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to First Years Only (FYC)
📖 Description
When we think of evil, we often imagine Hollywood-style movie villains, people with malicious intent and genius plans to destroy the world. When we look through history, we often find that evil is much more complicated. In many cases, it is perpetrated by ordinary people who have unthinkingly adopted abhorrent views and practices accepted by their societies. The goals for this course are to ask whether we have unreflectively accepted any such views and practices, to determine what the appropriate responses to evil are once we've recognized it and to practice making the world a better place. Topics include: the nature of evil, global justice, animal suffering, treatment of the elderly, civil disobedience, and beauty standards.

PHIL 200-01: Critical Reasoning

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Pearson P
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs. & Sophomores and 1st years Not Open to Those Who Took PHIL 100W. Not open to students who have taken PHIL-100.
📖 Description
This course will introduce students to both the formal study of logic and argumentation and to a wide range of creative (and ingenious!) arguments from across the history of philosophy.

PHIL 202W-01: Eastern Philosophy

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Edwards D
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📖 Description
What is the self? What is the good life for a human being? What is the relationship between humans and nature? Are all things interconnected? What is the universe fundamentally like? In this course we will explore how these questions have been addressed in Eastern philosophy, and see how life's great mysteries can be explored in a variety of ways by engaging in the numerous philosophical methods found in Eastern thought. Typical focus is on key philosophical texts from China, India, and Japan, and views often discussed include Confucianism, Daoism, Buddhism, and the various metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical aspects of different versions of these theories.

PHIL 203-01: History of Modern Western Philosophy

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM @ KRJH 236
👤 Instructor: Marcus R
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Philosophy (PHIL)
📖 Description
A survey of themes in the works of some major philosophers of the 17th and 18th centuries in Europe, taught using team-based learning. Spurred by advances in science and criticisms of Church dogma, philosophers in the modern era attempted to reconcile the scientific revolution with a broad view of human abilities. They constructed systematic views of the world and our place in it in order to answer big questions, including ones about appearance and reality, the relation between minds and bodies, the nature of knowledge, God, laws of nature, and free will.

PHIL 230-01: Philosophy of Sport

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Edwards D
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📖 Description
Examining the nature and value of sport. We explore how key philosophical themes such as meaning, identity, morality, freedom, justice, and reality play out in sport. Examples of issues discussed include what sport is, and what makes an activity a sport; the connection between sport and the good life; the nature of rules and their application in sports; the identity of sports teams over time; whether players have a duty to play fair; the ethics of technological enhancement; equality of opportunity and competition; and the relationship between sport and art.

PHIL 234-01: Our Shared World

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Amico-Korby D
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One 100 level course in Philosophy
📖 Description
Most people think animals deserve some moral consideration---it would be wrong to kick your dog for no reason. But what is the nature and weight of this consideration? We will study 3 philosophical topics with the aim of answering this question. (1) What are animal minds like? Can they grieve, do they have a sense of justice, do shrimp feel pain? (2) How do we resolve inconsistencies in the ways we view animals? We eat pigs and cows, but not dogs and horses. We treat lab rats according to stringent ethical guidelines, but painfully poison them when they get in our homes. And (3) how should we relate to wild animals? Should we conserve species? Should we bring back mammoths and saber-toothed cats? Should we prevent the suffering of wild animals?

PHIL 237W-01: Aesthetics

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Pearson P
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📖 Description
This course will introduce students to debates that are central to aesthetics and the philosophy of art. We will consider issues such as what makes something a work of art, why we should engage with works of art, whether beauty really is in the eye of the beholder, and what to do about works of art by morally problematic artists.

PHIL 242W-01: The Black Self: Identity and Consciousness

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Franklin A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: AFRST-242
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Philosophy (PHIL) or Africana Studies (AFRST), or consent of instructor
📖 Description
A philosophical exploration of a variety of historical and contemporary works that illuminate and influence the phenomenological experience of being black.

PHIL 314W-01: Literary Philosophers

Philosophy  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Janack M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Philosophy (PHIL), Literature (LIT), Creative Writing (CRWR) or consent of instructor
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, and Soph
📖 Description
What does writing style have to do with philosophical content? We will look at the "old quarrel" between the philosophers and the poets, and look at the ways in which philosophy was and is written, to think about what counts as philosophy and why and how we mark it off from its others. Readings by Borges, Calvino, Kafka, Coetzee, Plato and others.

PHIL 414-01: Knowledge and its Limits

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ PHIL 109
👤 Instructor: Pearson P
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in philosophy or permission of the instructor.
📖 Description
An advanced study of analytic epistemology. We will explore contemporary debates about the nature of knowledge, evidence, justification, the structure of the mind, and the significance of truth.

PHIL 416-01: Wittgenstein

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ PHIL 109
👤 Instructor: Marcus R
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or permission of instructor
💬 Comments: Taught in alternating years.
📖 Description
A broad study of themes through Wittgenstein’s work, including the picture-theory, naming, rule-following, meaning, skepticism, and truth. While our focus will be on Wittgenstein’s work, we will also spend time on his intellectual forebears and those he influenced, including Frege, Russell, Anscombe, Quine, Kripke, and Diamond.

PHIL 430-01: Plato

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Clark J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in Philosophy (PHIL) or PHIL-201
📖 Description
An intensive study of the philosophical dialogues of Plato, exploring interpretive matters, historical settings, philosophical arguments, and dramatic features. Special attention will be given to the primary texts, and some time and attention will be spent discussing secondary literature. The course will span every major area of philosophy (including metaphysics, ethics, epistemology, aesthetics, and logic) just as the works of Plato do.

PHIL 443-01: Detachment

Philosophy  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ PHIL 109
👤 Instructor: Edwards D
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Three courses in Philosophy or consent of the instructor
📖 Description
How much should we care about what happens in our lives? If we care too much, we risk being mired in anxiety and pain, but if we care too little, we seem to lose something central to our humanity. In this seminar we will explore how various philosophical traditions and ages, from East to West, from Ancient to Contemporary, have aimed to resolve this issue through the notion of detachment. We will consider how detachment—in its various forms—can form a central part of a good human life. We also explore critiques of detachment by examining its connections to authenticity and alienation. Examples of traditions to be explored include Stoicism, Epicureanism, Daoism, Buddhism, Existentialism, and Absurdism.

PHYS 136-01: Physics and Art

Physics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 12:00 PM – 12:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Brown K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 11, Jr: 12, Sr: 12]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr Familiarity with algebra and calculus recommended.
📖 Description
This course is a survey of some of the interesting ways in which fine art intersects math and physics. The curriculum consists of six topics in which some juxtaposition of physics and art is present; in some cases physics is relevant to the context of the art, in some case to the content of the art, and in some cases, both. We begin with some of the earliest works of art and proceed chronologically, including cave paintings and radiocarbon dating, the Archimedes palimpsest and imaging techniques, and the drip paintings of Jackson Pollock and their connection to chaotic motion and fractals.

PHYS 295-01: Electromagnetism

Physics  •  1 Credit

Physics  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ SCCT G047

PHYS 340-01: Topics in Quantum Physics

📖 Description
Exploration of topics in contemporary physics using the tools of quantum mechanics developed in PHYS-290. Topics may include multi-electron atoms, molecules, solid state physics, lasers and quantum optics, nuclear physics, quantum computing, and particle physics.

PHYS 348-01: Science, Technology, and Society

Physics  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Brewer K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: CHEM-348
📋 Prerequisites: Restricted to Chemistry or Physics concentrators or permission of the instructor.
💬 Comments: Restricted to CHEM and PHYS majors. 0.5 credit class; Runs from 1/20/27 to 3/12/27.
📖 Description
An examination of the assumptions, paradigms, and hierarchies embedded in science and technology. This course will examine evidence pointing to the structure of hierarchies built into and from science and how those structures may result in inequalities for various groups participating in and affected by science and technology. Topics will vary but might include: the objectivity/subjectivity of science; how biases and social structures intersect with equity, diversity, and inclusion in science; and gender and race disparities in STEM fields.

PHYS 349-01: Science, Technology, and Society II

Physics  •  0.5 Credits

In addition to an in-depth case study, students will complete projects using their knowledge of social, structural, and institutional hierarchies to improve the Physics Department.

PPOL 101-01: Introduction to Law

🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM

👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]

📖 Description
Focus on the American system of law: principally constitutional law, criminal law, and the development of civil rights. Topics include philosophical approaches to justice, English common law, and comparative analysis of French civil law and legal codes in socialist political systems and in majority Muslim countries. Attention also to legal regimes regarding refugees, Native Americans, and defendants with mental illness.

🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: List A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: NEURO-204
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-101, PSYCH-105, or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109
📖 Description
Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a behavioral and cognitive perspective. Survey of experimental and clinical research involving humans and non-human animals, addressing presumed neural mechanisms for cognitive, motivational and emotional states. Analysis of amnesia, aphasia, agnosias, apraxias and disconnection syndromes.

PSYCH 204-02: Fundamentals of Human Neuroscience

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: List A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: NEURO-204
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-101, PSYCH-105, or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109
📖 Description
Introduction to the field of neuroscience from a behavioral and cognitive perspective. Survey of experimental and clinical research involving humans and non-human animals, addressing presumed neural mechanisms for cognitive, motivational and emotional states. Analysis of amnesia, aphasia, agnosias, apraxias and disconnection syndromes.

PSYCH 254-01: Counseling Psychology

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 8:00 AM – 10:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Warden K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-101; PSYCH-105; or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the Psychology or Neuroscience concentration or the Psychology minor.
📖 Description
An overview of the theoretical orientations, treatment approaches and empirical literature in the field of counseling psychology. Examines the mechanisms by which counseling interventions facilitate personal and interpersonal functioning with a focus on emotional, social, educational, vocational and developmental concerns.

PSYCH 267-01: Psychological Bias in the Justice System

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Williams K
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-101, PSYCH-105, or PSYCH-109 / NEURO-109
💬 Comments: The 200-level of this course is open to Spring 2027 Justice Lab students only. Not open to students who have taken PSYCH 367.
📖 Description
How does group membership (e.g., sex, race, mental health status) shape one's experiences with the criminal justice system? Adopting a chronological approach through an exemplar criminal case (e.g., arrest, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, sentencing, release), this course will use case law and empirical research to explore the law's continuing efforts - and shortcomings - in addressing and decreasing bias. Does not count toward the Psychology or Neuroscience concentration or the Psychology minor.

PSYCH 321W-01: Psychology of Gender and Leadership

Psychology  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM  |  Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Adjei Boateng F
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-201/ NEURO-201
💬 Comments: Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory work.
📖 Description
Theoretical and methodological examination of how leadership potential is socially constructed, evaluated, and rewarded, and how these processes are shaped by gender stereotypes. Topics include leadership prototypes, role congruity and lack-of-fit models, backlash and bias, intersectionality, and the effects of gender and race on leadership evaluations. Class time is devoted to in-depth analysis of research articles and case studies, along with student-led discussions and presentations. Laboratory component involves two original research projects with data collection, statistical analysis, scholarly writing, and oral presentations.

PSYCH 329-01: Stress and Psychophysiology

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM  |  Mon 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Faig K
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: NEURO-329
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201 and PSYCH-204 / NEURO-204 or PSYCH-205 / NEURO-205
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology. (Same as PSYCH-329, NEURO-329.)
📖 Description
A theoretical and methodological exploration of the psychological and physiological mechanisms of stress. Questions will include: How does psychological stress impact health and well-being? What neurobiological mechanisms are involved? What is the role of environmental context? Laboratory exercises will include designing original experiments to examine the role of stress on behavior and physiological activity, as well as analyzing data, writing papers based on findings, and oral and poster presentations. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

PSYCH 330-01: Systems Neuroscience

Psychology  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM  |  Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 3087
👤 Instructor: Myers A
👥 Capacity: 10 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: BIO-330, NEURO-330
📋 Prerequisites: Take BIO-205 / NEURO-205 / PSYCH-205
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.
📖 Description
The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

PSYCH 330-02: Systems Neuroscience

Psychology  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,LAB
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM  |  Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ SCCT 3087
👤 Instructor: Myers A
👥 Capacity: 10 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: BIO-330, NEURO-330
📋 Prerequisites: Take BIO-205 / NEURO-205 / PSYCH-205
💬 Comments: Does not count toward the lab requirement in Psychology.
📖 Description
The primary focus of this course is on the physiological and chemical basis of behavior from a systems perspective. Topics include analysis of sensory and motor systems; motivated behaviors; stress, anxiety and mental illness; and learning and memory. Laboratory exercises introduce students to the anatomy and physiology of the mammalian central nervous system and to some of the principal techniques used in systems and behavioral neuroscience. Three hours of class and three hours of laboratory.

PSYCH 337-01: Psychology of Friendship

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Williams K
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-201 or NEURO-201
📖 Description
An exploration of theoretical and empirical research on the psychology of friendship, with an emphasis on sociocultural and evolutionary approaches. We will consider questions such as: What is friendship, and what functions does it serve in our lives? How do we seek and maintain friendships? In what ways is friendship similar and different across cultures? Through activities and reflections, students will use course material as a lens for examining their own important relationships.

PSYCH 353-01: Adult Psychopathology

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: McKee T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201
📖 Description
Introduction to the study of mental disorders in adults, including historical and cultural perspectives. Focus on classification, diagnostic assessment, etiology, treatment, and evaluation of treatment efficacy for the major disorders including anxiety, affective, thought, substance, and eating disorders. Research methods in clinical psychology emphasized. Discussion will include how gender, race, ethnicity, culture, sexuality, and social class relate to our understanding of mental illness and its treatment.

PSYCH 367-01: Psychological Bias in the Justice System

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Williams K
👥 Capacity: 24 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201
💬 Comments: Not open to students who have taken PSYCH 267.
📖 Description
How does group membership (e.g., sex, race, ethnicity, religion) shape one’s experiences with the criminal justice system? Adopting a chronological approach through an exemplar criminal case (e.g., arrest, arraignment, plea bargaining, trial, sentencing, release), this course will use case law and empirical research to explore the law’s continuing efforts—and shortcomings—in addressing and decreasing bias.

PSYCH 379-01: Lifespan Development

Psychology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: White R
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: EDUC-379
📋 Prerequisites: PSYCH-201 / NEURO-201
📖 Description
An introduction to the science of lifespan development, from conception and prenatal development to older age and death. Focuses on multiple domains of development, including cognitive, social, physical, and emotional, with emphasis on how development in all domains is shaped by both biological and social/cultural influences (e.g., gender norms, social class, stereotyping and prejudice).

RELST 111W-01: Ancient Jewish Wisdom

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: JWST-111
📖 Description
An introduction to the Jewish Tradition and Jewish way of reading.

RELST 131-01: Religion and Ecology

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Lin N
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
This course explores ‘Religion and Ecology,’ beginning from a North American starting point in the 1960s amidst a budding environmentalist movement. Readings explore how mainly Christian theological communities engaged with a new social movement, before broadening to other religious traditions. The course then proceeds via a new theoretical frame: the religious lives of human communities are located within deep time and geographical space, with an eye to the migration history of the human as a natural kind. Along the way, we responsibly speculate about communities located in (what is now) Africa, the Middle East, Europe, Asia, and the Americas. The course ends by asking: how are we to live into a shared environmental future, and what is the role of our deepest religious commitments?

RELST 143W-01: The Sacred in South Asia

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Amar A
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-143
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Years, Sophomores, & Juniors
📖 Description
What constitutes the sacred in south Asia? Is it a person, place, river, hill, temple or nature/ecology? Where and how did the notion of sacrality emerge in South Asia? Is it linked exclusively to religious institutions or is it found in the daily lives of people? This course will examine these questions by exploring the multiple religious traditions of South Asia and examining their essential beliefs, doctrines, institutions, rituals and popular practices through a study of texts, material culture, films and ethnographic accounts.

RELST 145-01: World Films, World Faiths

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Rodriguez-Plate S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 10, Sr: 0]
🔀 Cross-listed: CNMS-145
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Sophomores, & Juniors Evening film screenings.
📖 Description
Introduces the practices and beliefs of several major world religions (including Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism) through the medium of film. Exploring Japanese anime, Indonesia documentaries, video films from Ghana, Bollywood mythologicals, Jesus-films from Latin America, Korean-Buddhist films, contemporary fictional glimpses into Jewish life, and more, shows how religious people live and struggle and find joy, by using the audio-visual medium of film.

RELST 146W-01: Medieval Christianities

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Eldevik J
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-146, MDRST-146
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Sophomores, & 1st Yrs Open to First and Second Year Students Only.
📖 Description
A survey of the development of the Christian religion in premodern Eurasia and the Mediterranean, from its elevation to a state cult in the later Roman Empire to about 1450. Special consideration will be given to the growth of the church and processes of conversion, the problem of authority versus heresy and heterodoxy, and the relationship of the Christian churches to Islam and other non-Christian peoples. Stress on basic skills in the study of history.

RELST 198-01: Readings in Religious Studies

Religious Studies  •  0.25 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Wed 12:00 PM – 12:50 PM
👤 Instructor: Rodriguez-Plate S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to Srs, Jrs, Soph, & 1st Years Students may take this course as many times as desired.
📖 Description
Religious Studies faculty join with students to read and discuss one important and/or provocative work each semester.

RELST 207-01: The Social Lives of the Ancient Dead

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Persad S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: CLASC-207
💬 Comments: (Application, Interpretation)
📖 Description
What happened to people after they died in the ancient world? Often, their story was only beginning. This course looks at the ways the dead remained part of everyday life. We will read curse tablets that call on restless spirits, laws about stolen bodies, stories about cities fighting over heroic bones, and Christian accounts of remains that heal or protect the living. We will also study tombs and inscriptions to see how people used the dead to make claims about family, memory, status, and belonging. The course ends close to home. For the final project, students will turn to Hamilton’s own cemetery and investigate how one grave, monument, or burial story creates a social life for the dead on our campus. The larger question throughout the course is simple: what can the dead still do for the living?

RELST 208W-01: Asian Temples in a Digital World

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Wilson T
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-208, HIST-208
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Asian Studies, History, or Religious Studies
📖 Description
Examination of three aspects of Asian religions: temple as built space, ritual object (e.g., image, talisman, offering, etc.), and ritual practice as intentional use of objects and space. Students work in groups to research an Asian temple of their choice and curate a web-based exhibition of the history of and ritual practices conducted in their temple. Instruction in digital tools of collecting, analyzing, and representing materials in a web-based exhibition. Writing assignments include short essays and a final research project of the student’s design to be presented with text and images in digital form.

RELST 210-01: Minorities in the Middle East: History, Religion, and Relations with Political Powers

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Amir S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ARABC-210, MEIWS-210
📖 Description
This course explores how minority communities in the Middle East—Druze, ʿAlawites, Kurds, Yezidis, Armenians, Maronites, Copts, Assyrians, and others—have been formed and transformed from the late Ottoman era to the present. Beginning with the shift from imperial pluralism to nation-state “minorities,” it examines how religion, identity, nationalism, and political power shape communal identity and minority–state relations. Case studies span Lebanon, Syria, Israel, Turkey, Iran, Iraq, and Egypt, addressing genocide, displacement, nationalism, citizenship, security, and diaspora. Drawing on history, anthropology, religious studies, and political science, students examine how communities negotiate identity, power, and recognition in a plural Middle East. This course examines historical and contemporary experiences of minority communities in the Middle East. Some course materials address difficult subjects, including genocide, mass violence, persecution, forced displacement, sexual violence, religious and ethnic discrimination, and war. These topics are approached in their historical and scholarly contexts and are essential to understanding the experiences of the communities studied in the course.

RELST 261-01: Jewish Feminism

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: JWST-261
📖 Description
This course examines the foundational texts, debates, and activism of Jewish feminism in the United States from the early 1970s to the present. Students will explore how Jewish women named and theorized gender inequality in Jewish law, ritual, theology, communal life, and cultural practice—and how those critiques reshaped American Judaism. Readings will situate Jewish feminist thought within wider developments in feminist, religious, and American social history. The course also considers LGBTQ Jewish ideas and activism, asking where they converge with, extend, or challenge Jewish feminist concerns. Students will gain a vocabulary for analyzing the movement’s central questions, historical evolution, and enduring impact on Jewish life today.

RELST 263-01: American Jewish Literature

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Steiner B
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: JWST-263, LIT-263
📖 Description
What makes a work “Jewish American literature”? Must it be written by a Jewish author, center Jewish characters or themes, or appear in a Jewish language? This course uses such questions to explore the American Jewish experience from the earliest Jewish settlement to the present, with particular attention to the period after 1865. Through fiction, poetry, memoir, drama, and other genres, students will examine how writers have represented migration, religion, family, race, belonging, assimilation, and cultural difference. Rather than imposing fixed definitions, the course treats “Jewish,” “American,” and “literature” as contested categories whose meanings have changed over time.

RELST 267-01: Conspiracy Theories and Religion

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: King S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Apocalyptic visions, prophecies, and experiences of revelation have mobilized, challenged, and sustained the commitment of religious believers and conspiracy theorists alike. But what else do conspiracy theories and religions share in common, and how do they differ? This course explores intersections of religion and conspiracy theories in American culture from the 19th century to the present day. We examine historical materials alongside contemporary analyses, including millennialist tracts and sermons, conspiracy theory message board websites, illustrations of biblical prophecies, and pictograms of apocalyptic visions. Along the way, we consider how categorizations of “conspiracy theories” and “fringe” movements have served as critical sites for theorizing and delimiting the margins of “real” religion and acceptable belief.

RELST 269-01: Buddhist Environmentalism

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Lin N
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs (Location)
📖 Description
This course explores the conjunction of Buddhism and environmentalism. Part I considers advocates of this combination, or “eco-Buddhists,” with a focus on those who criticize current structures of political economy. Classical texts from the Buddhist canon (Nagarjuna, the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, etc.) will be introduced with an eye to seeing where eco-Buddhists derive some of their core claims. Part II considers critics of eco-Buddhists, who raise the objection that historical Buddhists never held commitments like those of modern-day environmentalists. Could eco-Buddhism even be a new form of Orientalism? The course concludes by making sense of these critiques on the way to a historically responsible description of what a modern Buddhist environmentalism might be.

RELST 271-01: Mother Nature—Climate Crisis—Jainism

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Costello C
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: ASNST-271
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr No prior coursework on Religion or Asia is required.
📖 Description
How have people in India understood and interacted with mother nature? How do they conceptualize the environment and ecosystems? How do they deal with climate change and ecological disasters? What role does religion play in shaping human attitude to the mother nature? Focusing on Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, the course examines how Indian communities have engaged and negotiated their relationships with the natural world to consider themes including the conception of environment as sacred space, ethical living, non-violence, animal-protection, and food-culture.

RELST 291-01: Imagining Religions

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Rodriguez-Plate S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 0, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 4]
📋 Prerequisites: One 100-level Religious Studies course
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors, Juniors, & Sophomores
📖 Description
Students will learn to imagine, analyze, and interpret religion(s) in a wide variety of ways. Students will engage critically with the category of "religion" and related concepts such as sacred space, the other, colonialism, modernity, globalization, and comparison.

RELST 312-01: Religion and Magic

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: King S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One Religious Studies course
📖 Description
Hypnotism. Stage magic. Wonder shows. What do these things have to do with religion? This course explores this question as we trace various intersections of magic and religion from the 18th century to the present day, examining topics including occult and esoteric movements, conjuring practices, mesmerism, hypnotism, spiritualism, telepathy, and stage magic performances. Throughout this course, we engage with critical theories and methods in the study of religion that shed light on the religious dimensions of magic and magical dynamics of religion. In addition to scholarly works from the fields of religious studies and cultural history, we examine a range of cultural data and historical artifacts, from colonial-era trials against alleged sorcerers to 20 th century scientific experiments in psychic phenomena.

RELST 318-01: How Satan Became the Devil

Religious Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Persad S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
💬 Comments: (Application, Interpretation)
📖 Description
Satan does not enter history as the horned ruler of hell we recognize today. This course follows how a relatively minor figure in early Jewish traditions became Christianity’s great enemy of God. Along the way, we will meet fallen angels who teach humans forbidden knowledge, demons who possess bodies, monks who claim to wrestle with the Devil in the desert, and exorcists trying to identify what has taken control of a person. We will also see how Satan became connected to heresy, witchcraft, and fears about the end of the world. Rather than treating the Devil as one unchanging character, we will ask why different societies kept reinventing him. Students will explore a larger question: what does a culture reveal about itself when it decides what evil looks like?

RSNST 222-01: Modern Russian History

Translation  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Keller S
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: HIST-222
📖 Description
An overview of Russian history from the emancipation of the serfs to the collapse of the Soviet Union. Themes of the course include how Russia and the USSR dealt with their sense of "backwardness" compared to Europe, the multi-national and multi-religious nature of this vast Eurasian state, and the meanings of "modernity."

RSNST 227-01: Literature and Revolution: Twentieth- and Twenty-First Century Russian and Soviet Fiction.

Translation  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Cieply J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
💬 Comments: Taught in English. No knowledge of Russian required.
📖 Description
This course offers a survey of twentieth- and twenty-first-century Russian and Soviet fiction, focusing on the literature that defined this transformative period in Russia’s modern history.

RSNST 237-01: Russia and the World

Russian Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Rivera D
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 15, So: 15, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
🔀 Cross-listed: GOVT-237
📋 Prerequisites: Take any one of the following: GOVT-112, GOVT-114, one Russian Studies course, or consent of instructor.
💬 Comments: (International Relations)
📖 Description
The course will examine Russia’s relations with both its post-Soviet neighbors and the West from the Tsarist era to the present. Topics to be covered include: the formation of the Russian Empire, the Cold War, the evolution of Russian-Western relations since the collapse of communism, Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, and the outbreak of a major war with Ukraine in 2022. A central theme of the course will be the evolution of Russian national identity, especially as it relates to Russia’s status as an empire and its relationship with the West.

RSNST 262-01: Siberian Text

Translation  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Abrahamyan A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: AIIS-262, LIT-262
💬 Comments: Taught in English.
📖 Description
This course is an exploration of five centuries of writing in and about Siberia. While we will root ourselves in the socio-historical context, our main goal is to engage meaningfully with the very process of the formation of the Siberian Text. By this, scholars of the region mean the body of works that emerged out of the geographical, political, anthropological, and cultural categorizations of Siberia. The plurality of voices and the diversity of spatial experiences engaged in the process of creating the Siberian Text include travelers, criminals, political prisoners, religious dissenters, shamans, hunters, ethnographers, missionaries, vagabonds, and peasants. Probing the fraught legacy of the current spatial discourse on Siberia, the course will examine a variety of media and genres, including official documents, travelogues, oral tradition(s), works of fiction, autobiographies, pictorial art, and film. In addition to the transnational and transhistorical dimensions, we will engage with theories of space and place, imagined geographies, and ecocriticism.

RUSSN 120-01: Second-Term Russian

Russian Language  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,1 HOUR TBA
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Cieply J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: RUSSN-110 or equivalent
📖 Description
Continued development of skills in spoken and written Russian. Intensive use of audio/visual and computer materials.

RUSSN 220-01: Fourth-Term Russian

Russian Language  •  1 Credit  •  LEC,1 HOUR TBA
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed/Fri 11:00 AM – 11:50 AM
👤 Instructor: Abrahamyan A
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: RUSSN-210 or equivalent
📖 Description
Continuation of third-term Russian. Introduction to the language of popular culture, including contemporary film and music.

RUSSN 380-01: Advanced Russian II

Russian Language  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Cieply J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: RUSSN-220 or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Continuation of Russian Studies 370. The focus of this class will be on writing, reading, and talking about daily life, or "byt" in diary form, broadly conceived. Works of literature and culture will be compared with social media posts in both long (blog posts) and short formats (memes, tweets, tik toks, etc). Advanced readings and discussion will be accompanied by a thorough review of grammar and difficult grammar points.

SOC 101-01: Introductory Sociology

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 8:30 AM – 9:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Sacco T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 20, So: 20, Jr: 0, Sr: 0]
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs and Sophomores Only Not Open to Those Who Took Soc 110 Not open to students who have taken SOC-110.
📖 Description
Sociological perspective on human behavior. Classic and contemporary sociological concepts that further an understanding of the structure, process, stability and change of social life.

SOC 126-01: The Sociology of Health and Illness

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Grace M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This course will give students an introduction to the sociological study of health and illness. While sociologists have taken the study of medicine seriously since at least the 1950s, health and illness are phenomena whose relationship to human society and experience are long and complex. In order to explore this reality, this class will draw on the empirical work of historians, anthropologists, sociologists, and even fiction writers to explore the personal and social elements of sickness and health.

SOC 212-01: Sociology of Elites

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Ercan H
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
💬 Comments: Retakeable up to two times.
📖 Description
Who rules—and how do they stay on top? This course examines inequality from above, exploring how elites are formed, legitimated, and challenged across diverse settings. Case studies range from Ivy League admissions and Wall Street hiring to technology elites, Russian oligarchs, emergent Chinese elites, Indian caste hierarchies, and royal families in the Gulf. We will explore how class, race, and gender shape the formation of elite groups, their capacity to appropriate resources, and their struggles with rival elites over power and resources. By the end of the course, students will have the analytical tools to understand not just who holds power, but how that power is reproduced, justified, and contested.

SOC 217-01: Sociology of Education

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Stewart M
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
🔀 Cross-listed: EDUC-217
📋 Prerequisites: SOC-101, SOC-110, or SOC-126
📖 Description
This course provides a sociological lens for analyzing education and educational inequality in the United States. Over the course of the semester, we will use various theories to explore education as a social institution, going beyond our own individual experiences and personal ideologies. In addition to covering the foundational ideas in the sociology of education, we will spend considerable time exploring the myriad ways that education impacts, and is impacted by, broader patterns of inequality. We will also use empirical studies to examine external factors that affect student experiences and shape learning outcomes; factors such as the role of families, neighborhoods, and schools, themselves. Salient topics include racial segregation, economic stratification within and between schools, technology, tracking, teacher pedagogy, immigration, English Language Learners, punishment, higher education, and the future of education in a demographically and culturally diversifying society.

SOC 224-01: Crime, Law, and Inequality

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Ercan H
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This course examines crime, criminalization, and social control from a sociological perspective. Rather than treating crime as simply the violation of law, we examine how crime is socially and politically constructed and how practices of punishment and regulation emerge through broader struggles over power, morality, and social order. Topics include moral panics, addiction and criminalization, policing and surveillance, mass incarceration, organized crime, mafia networks, illicit drug economies, corporate crime, state violence, terrorism, and border enforcement. Students will critically evaluate competing explanations of crime and examine how criminalization and social control both shape and are shaped by relations of power, inequality, governance, and social change.

SOC 228-01: Work, Organizations, and Inequality

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Sacco T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📖 Description
This course will examine how complex organizations structure work in the United States, how work has changed, and why. We will examine the structure of work from an organizational perspective, which introduces students to a framework for thinking about how social institutions (such as federal policies or racial inequality) shape the experiences of the everyday people. Students will begin to deepen their knowledge about the structure of work in the U.S., why it looks the way that it does today, and who benefits (or does not benefit) from this system.

SOC 256-01: Sociology of Immigration

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Selzer J
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats [Fr: 10, So: 10, Jr: 10, Sr: 10]
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Sociology (SOC) or consent of instructor
📖 Description
This course examines international migration as a social process, with a main focus on immigration to the United States. It provides sociological perspectives to understand why immigration happens, how it occurs, and what consequences and outcomes it produces. We will explore theories of migration and compare and contrast trends in old world and new world migration systems, as well as the American migration experience.

SOC 276W-01: Global Commemoration: Remembering the Unspeakable

Sociology  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Selzer J
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: SOC-101, SOC-110, or SOC-126
📖 Description
This course examines how atrocities - big and small - are remembered around the globe: What is the process through which individual experiences are transformed into credible testimonies and collective traumas? What role do state actors, educational institutions, community organizations, and civic society play in the production of memory? And what is the purpose of keeping the past alive if societies are ever-changing and evolving? We will trace the long-lasting legacies of human brutality to different parts of the globe. By listening to survivors, exploring different forms of testimonies, and combing through evidence accumulated by investigative journalists, we will critically engage with and expand upon foundational sociological texts on history, memory, and commemoration.

SOC 301W-01: Sociological Theory

Sociology  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Ellingson S
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Two Sociology (SOC) courses
📖 Description
Examination of classic and contemporary sociological concepts and perspectives. The theorists covered include Marx, Weber, Durkheim, Freud, Mead, Berger and Luckmann, and Foucault.

SOC 305-01: Urban America

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Selzer J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Sociology (SOC) or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Although globalization scholars at the turn of the millennium predicted the loss of importance of the local, cities have continued to be vital anchors of social, economic, political, and cultural life. While they may serve as a safe haven for some, they are simultaneously the site of continuous political struggles over the boundaries of belonging. Tracing the history of urbanization in the U.S., this course explores various facets of contemporary urban life, including urban disempowerment, poverty, segregation, and gentrification. At the same time, we will look at the many ways in which residents – including migrants and members of the LGBTQIA+ community – claim their right to the city.

SOC 315-01: Sociology of Violence

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Ercan H
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: Students must have taken SOC-101, SOC-110, or SOC-126
📖 Description
Violence is deeply intertwined with power, inequality, and struggles among social groups, political movements, and the state. It ranges from direct physical harm to structural and symbolic forms that often go unrecognized as violence at all. This course traces how power inequalities enable violence and its erasure, and how state and nonstate violence interact to reproduce or reshape those inequalities. Using a comparative global approach, we examine specific sites and collective contentious events where these dynamics become visible, from prisons and borders to war and militarized conflict, genocide, torture, counterinsurgency, terrorism, and counterrevolution.

SOC 325-01: Medicine in America

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Wed/Fri 2:30 PM – 3:45 PM
👤 Instructor: Grace M
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: SOC-101
📖 Description
We take for granted medicine as we know it today, yet at the turn of the 20th century, medical practice could have taken any number of directions. Why did allopathic medicine win out over its competitors to consolidate professional and cultural authority over health? How has the patient-provider relationship evolved from an asymmetric model to one characterized by patient consumerism? How do trainees learn medicine’s “hidden curriculum”? Looking forward, how will providers fare against challenges to autonomy posed by insurance companies, for-profit hospitals, politicians, and AI? To answer these and related questions, this course draws on empirical studies, historical accounts, and media to examine how the profession of medicine has been constructed, contested, and transformed over time.

SOC 329-01: Seminar on the Social Production of Food

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM
👤 Instructor: Ellingson S
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One Sociology (SOC) course
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., and Sophomores
📖 Description
Examines the production and consumption of food in contemporary societies from a sociological perspective. We will study how food shapes personal identity and communal life; the organizational and institutional contexts food production from farm to table; the role food plays in popular culture and the rise of alternative food movements. Covers such topics as food, communal identity and family; the culture and practices of "Foodies"; the world of the restaurant kitchen; globalization and changes in farming and food consumption.

SOC 342-01: Sociology of Climate Change and Climate Action

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Strong A, Kucinskas J
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: ENVST-342
📋 Prerequisites: One course in Environmental Studies or Sociology
📖 Description
In the face of the ongoing climate crisis, we are also witnessing deployment of climate solutions: electrification of transportation, renewable energy development, reforestation initiatives, and reductions in animal agriculture. How do communities react to these approaches to climate action? We unpack theoretical and on-the-ground perspectives on what climate change means among different groups of people and explore people’s social location influences how they understand and respond to it individually and collectively. We examine how colonialism, and macroeconomic structures shape perspectives on the experience of the climate crisis and responses to it. Students apply their theoretical understanding in structured community conversations about climate solutions with community stakeholders.

SOC 351-01: AI and Society

Sociology  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM
👤 Instructor: Sacco T
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: One intro-level sociology course
📖 Description
Artificial Intelligence (AI) will shape society in profound ways, disrupting fields like higher education, government, science, or medicine. Yet integrating AI responsibly into society remains difficult. This course explores the sociological dimensions of AI, from its historical roots to today's debates around bias, autonomy, and changing human relationships. Students will critically examine how AI systems perceive, reason, and communicate, with emphasis on machine learning's role in driving AI capabilities. The course also unpacks the politics of algorithms, data, and code, and how AI is socially shaped in practice. Drawing on social science research on technology, work, media, and inequalities, students will investigate how AI can be developed and deployed in ways that align with human values and create meaningful social impact.

THETR 100-01: "Playing" Introduction to Making Theatre: Theory and Practice

Theatre  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ KTSA 219  |  Tue/Thu 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ KTSA 218
👤 Instructor: Harrison E
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats [Fr: 5, So: 5, Jr: 5, Sr: 5]
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yrs. One section for first-year students only; first-years and sophomores. Juniors with permission of the Department.
📖 Description
This is the gateway course for all theatre courses. This class combines the study of theatre and drama as it reflects, represents and interprets diverse cultures with a hands-on examination of how theatre is made. Through readings, lectures, discussions and projects the class will explore the ideas, strategies and languages of theatre (acting, directing, playwriting, designing) that theatre artists use to create contemporary theatrical performance.

THETR 102-01: Acting Workshop

Theatre  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ KTSA 218  |  Mon/Wed 1:00 PM – 2:15 PM @ KTSA 219
👤 Instructor: Cryer M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats [Fr: 8, So: 8, Jr: 0, Sr: 0]
📋 Prerequisites: THETR-100
📖 Description
Acting workshop is a critical level acting course that teaches students how to make strong acting choices by learning what questions to ask.

THETR 142-01: Production

Theatre  •  0.5 Credits
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Tue/Wed/Thu/Fri 4:15 PM – 7:00 PM @ KTSA 211  |  Mon/Tue/Wed/Thu/Fri 4:15 PM – 7:00 PM @ KTSA 217  |  Mon/Tue/Wed/Thu/Fri 4:15 PM – 7:00 PM @ KTSA 219
👤 Instructor: Buttery J, Harrison E, Ost T
👥 Capacity: 40 Seats
💬 Comments: Instructor's Signature Req. One-half credit. May be repeated for credit.
📖 Description
The study of theatre through participation (performance, management and/or technical work) in a faculty-directed production. Students must pre-register for this class; for 141F first-year students may register during orientation. Preregistration does not guarantee an acting role. Auditions will take place at the start of the semester, and students not acting will perform a technical/production role.

THETR 208-01: Stage Combat

Theatre  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 217  |  Fri 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 218
👤 Instructor: Drake J
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: THETR-100
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
This is a class on stage combat, armed and unarmed. How to safely fight on stage and make it look real.

THETR 213-01: Lighting Design

Theatre  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ KTSA 217
👤 Instructor: Buttery J
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
📋 Prerequisites: THETR-105
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
An in-depth exploration of lighting and projection design for live performance. The course will cover the process, techniques, equipment and methodologies of these theatre design disciplines. These include; composition, color theory, projection mapping, CAD drafting, as well as lighting for the camera.

THETR 215-01: Scene Painting

Theatre  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Fri 9:00 AM – 12:00 PM @ KTSA 217
👤 Instructor: Ost T
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 0, So: 4, Jr: 4, Sr: 4]
📋 Prerequisites: THETR-105, THETR-130, or a 100-level Art course
💬 Comments: Open to Seniors, Juniors, and Sophomores
📖 Description
Through a series of projects and demonstrations, introduces students to the basic principles ofscenic painting for film, television and the performing arts. Topics covered will include color mixing, texture,faux finishing (wood grain, marble, etc.), brush and spray techniques, trompe-l’oeil and large scale cartooning andpainting.

THETR 217-01: Stage Management

Theatre  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon 7:00 PM – 10:00 PM @ KTSA 220
👤 Instructor: Vangel M
👥 Capacity: 12 Seats [Fr: 3, So: 3, Jr: 3, Sr: 3]
📋 Prerequisites: THETR-100 or THETR-105
💬 Comments: Open to Srs., Jrs., Soph., & 1st Yr
📖 Description
Through this course students will learn the principles of stage management for theatrical productions. How to facilitate the needs of the production through each of its stages, create industry-standard procedures, paperwork, develop good communication/organizational skills as well as an appreciation of the tact/details that stage managers bring to each production.

THETR 231-01: Intermediate Media: New Frontiers in Storytelling

Theatre  •  1 Credit  •  STUDIO
🕒 Schedule: Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 143  |  Thu 1:00 PM – 4:00 PM @ KTSA 124
👤 Instructor: Huff A
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
🔀 Cross-listed: DARTS-231, MUSIC-231
📋 Prerequisites: Any intro-level Digital Arts studio course, including cross-listed.
💬 Comments: This course is part of the Spring 2027 Innovation Co-Lab
📖 Description
This class will survey and create emergent and non -linear forms of storytelling using digital and hybrid tools. We will examine notions of narrative authority and hybridity in a digital age and think through different ways we might use technology to distill, break apart or reify modes of communication and visual metaphor. Discussion will push boundaries of traditional storytelling and consider connectivity, liveness and embodied presence. This course will draw on multiple forms of expression including but not limited to digital media, performance, sound, XR, web, and network environments.

THETR 302-01: Advanced Acting Workshop: Shakespeare and Company

Theatre  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Mon/Wed 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ KTSA 217  |  Mon/Wed 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ KTSA 218  |  Mon/Wed 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM @ KTSA 219
👤 Instructor: Cryer M
👥 Capacity: 16 Seats
📋 Prerequisites: THETR-102 and THETR-201 or consent of instructor
📖 Description
Classical texts and contemporary performance. Focus on Shakespeare, language and character. May include other classical dramatists Scene and monologue work, textual analysis, vocal and speaking preparedness, verse and heightened speech, characterization, improvisation and rehearsals.

WMGST 101-01: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies

Women's and Gender Studies  •  1 Credit
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 9:00 AM – 10:15 AM
👤 Instructor: Singh T
👥 Capacity: 20 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only. This section is Speaking Intensive. May be offered as a standard course or FYC as well as writing intensive, non-writing intensive, or speaking intensive at the discretion of the department. Please check the schedule for details.
📖 Description
An interdisciplinary investigation of past and present views of women and their roles, treatment and experiences in institutions such as the family, the state, the work force, language and sexuality. The diversity of women’s experiences across age, class, ethnic, sexual, racial and national lines introduced, and theories of feminism and of women’s studies discussed.

WMGST 101W-01: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies

Women's and Gender Studies  •  1 Credit  •  Writing Intensive
🕒 Schedule: Tue/Thu 10:30 AM – 11:45 AM
👤 Instructor: Gentry M
👥 Capacity: 18 Seats
💬 Comments: Open to 1st Yrs, Soph. & Jrs. Only May be offered as a standard course or FYC as well as writing intensive, non-writing intensive, or speaking intensive at the discretion of the department. Please check the schedule for details.

An interdisciplinary investigation of past and present views of women and their roles, treatment and experiences in institutions such as the family, the state, the work force, language and sexuality. The diversity of women’s experiences across age, class, ethnic, sexual, racial and national lines introduced, and theories of feminism and of women’s studies discussed.

WMGST 101W-02: Introduction to Women's and Gender Studies
